subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my main criticism of the budget is that while it places the individual on a pay-as-you-go basis, it falls far short of placing the country on a similar basis, nor does it bring about a fairer distribution of the debt claims held against it.
The national debt is rapidly soaring. In 1939, at the beginning of the war, it stood at $3,152,000,000; to-day it is $7,861,000,000. And according to the minister's own estimate, by March of next year the debt will exceed $10,500,000,000. He has emphasized the fact that the national debt is largely held internally, and is therefore a debt unto ourselves. Unfortunately however, by far the greater proportion will be held in the hands of a comparatively few individuals, and therefore it will be necessary to tax all the people to pay tribute to this minority. That situation is being rapidly aggravated by our method of selling bonds. According to an article appearing in the Financial Post of January 16, giving a break-down of the second victory loan, it would appear that 339,000 individual $50 and $100 bonds have already been cashed. To overcome this unfavourable situation I would urge that a greater proportion of the taxation levied against people in the low income brackets should be in the form of compulsory savings, while on the other hand a greater proportion of the money borrowed from the people in the high income brackets should be obtained by taxation. By this means we could establish a fairer distribution of the debt claim held against the nation.
We have a ceiling on wages. We have a ceiling on prices. It is high time that, at least for the duration of the_war, we should have a ceiling on income. In my opinion that ceiling could very well be placed at a figure below $10,000. By that means I think we should at least aim at the principle of the equality of service and sacrifice.
For the next few moments I should like to deal with the two amendments before the house. First may I refer to the amendment moved by this group, as it appears at page 1092 of Hansard:
This house regrets that the government still disregards the possible uses of government-created national money to the end that in so far as taxation and the borrowing of the people's savings fail to meet government expenditures the government might employ national money:
(a)	To relieve the debt situation which threatens the ownership and control of a great many private businesses, factories, farms and other means of production.
(b)	To pay farmers and other primary producers fair prices, thereby stimulating the production of food.	_
(c)	To provide workers with adequate purchasing power.
(d)	To alleviate the distress of the aged and others in needy circumstances.
(e)	To prevent inflation by the subsidizing of industry where costs are uncontrollable, adopting where necessary a more aggressive and consistent rationing policy.
This amendment recognizes that a large percentage of production is required for war purposes, and that therefore it is necessary to curtail the people's spending power, by taxation, and the borrowing of the people's savings. It is advocated in the amendment that to the extent that taxation and the borrowing of savings has failed to meet government expenditures, national money should be used. In this instance the sum involved is $983,000,000. Of this amount, however, $790,000,000 is to be obtained from the chartered banks-or has been obtained, perhaps I should say. Only $193,000,000 has been obtained from the Bank of Canada.
I now turn to page 1106, and refer briefly to a criticism offered by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), where he states:
But if you are continually siphoning off, *what is the object of continually pouring in something you have to siphon off?
My chief objection to the hon. member's question is that it is likely to leave a totally wrong inference. Many people may jump to the conclusion that the hon. member has become a disciple of Charles Dunning, because time and again when I advocated before the war that national money should be used to put the unemployed to work, invariably that was the reply I got from Mr. Dunning. What is the sense of creating national money if you are going to have to tax it away, he used to ask. The Minister of Finance always told the house that the only money that was available to the government was the money they could tax out of the people's pockets. He refused to use national money, and the result was that we had half a million people unemployed. It would be just as sensible to say: Why pass water through a power plant when you are going to let it out at the other end? You pass water through and you pass money through your system in order that certain essential services may be performed; when it has completed those services, you get rid of it. If to-day the deficiency in revenue was not made up by national money or by an increase in money, what would happen? You would have undeveloped resources and idle men.
The Budget-Mr. Quelch

When, the minister of finance of New Zealand appeared before the committee on post-war reconstruction on May 22,1 asked this question and he made this answer:
Mr. Quelch: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if Mr. Nash would tell us what method of financing is used when taxation and public borrowings fail to meet government expenditures?
Hon. Mr. Nash: Well, the answer is inside a simple statement I made once in introducing the budget. If in connection with the production of the commodities that are necessary for ordinary human welfare the monetary means are not available to link unused resources with unused labour we, as a government, will find the money. We can do that because we are in control of the reserve bank; we can create our own money.
Some people will say that New Zealand is still operating under the capitalistic system, although it has a socialistic application, and that that policy would not be necessary in a socialist state. I want to emphasize the fact that it does not matter what kind of system you have in operation, whether capitalistic or a socialistic state; it will always be necessary from time to time to create new money in order to maintain the fullest development of your resources. May I in proof of that cite what has been happening in Russia, wdiich is a socialist country. I have in my hand a book entitled, "Russia's Economic Front for War and Peace" by Mr. Yugow. I shall refer particularly to the period before the war, because apparently the statistics for the war period are not available. This book is mainly a statistical summary of the economy of Russia.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In what year was the book published?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was published in 1942, but it is impossible to get accurate statistics for the years during the war. They were not being allowed out, but the League of Nations and other organizations figures were available up to 1938, which I think is the last year they were published.
The book emphasizes the fact that prior to 1937 Russia had begun to expand her economy at a tremendous rate, realizing as she did that she had not much time to accomplish what she was trying to accomplish, that is, to prepare to defend herself against both Japan and Germany. Her production had to be expanded very rapidly, and therefore a large percentage of the production of the country had to be taken away from the people in order to accomplish this end. Over twenty-six per cent of the production was appropriated for the purpose of expanding the industrialization of the country.
It is interesting to note the change of opinion which took place in Russia with regard to

money. In the days after the revolution there was a feeling that money was of little importance, and an attempt was made to do away entirely with the money system. The writer gives the viewpoint in Russia with regard to money when he says:
After some hesitation the communist economists have come to admit that money plays the decisive role in the economy of the country.
On page 144 it states:
. The quantity of newly emitted currency continued to grow rapidly.
That was in spite of the fact that very heavy taxation was being maintained. I want to put on the record figures from this book showing the amount of taxation and the amount of new money put out in certain years. In 1928 the total contribution to government, including all taxes and borrowings, amounted to 8-1 billion rubles, while in that year the issue of new money amounted to 2 billion rubles. In 1933 the total appropriations amount to 44-2 billion rubles while the issue of new money amount to 6-8 billion rubles. In 1938 the appropriations amounted to 127-5 billion rubles and the issue of new money to 11*25 billion rubles. While no figures are available for the war years, I -believe we will find that taxation has been increased still further and that the issue of money has been expanded tremendously. Inflation has been prevented.
I quote these figures merely to show that it does not matter what type of economy you have, whether it is capitalistic or socialistic, if you want to maintain the use of your resources at their full capacity you must issue new money continually in addition to your taxation and borrowing of the savings of the people.
The subamendment moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group reads: That all the words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for the nationalization of the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the w-ar;
and further this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their widows and dependents;
and further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance."
I am quite in accord with the substance of this amendment, but I regret that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation found it necessary to rule out our amendment in

The Budget-Mr. Quelch
proposing theirs. It is not easy to vote for an amendment which rules out your own amendment, even though you may be in accord with the substance of that amendment. I want to make it quite clear that I am heartily in accord with everything in this subamendment. I refer to what I said to this house on July 16, 1942, when, speaking on the question of obtaining effective control of our banking system, I said, as reported at page 4307 of Hansard:
I am of the opinion that the only fair and sound way to deal with the -whole question of effective control is to nationalize the chartered banks of Canada.
It might be well to remember that in New Zealand, although the government has been in power for a number of years, they still have not a national banking system. Apparently they have established effective control, but I am of the opinion that in order to have really effective control, in order to know just exactly what are the costs of handling the accounts of the nation, the banking system should be taken over.
At this time I should like to discuss the problem of agriculture, leaving my criticism of the budget until such time as the resolutions are before us.
There are those who say that at a time like this, when the world is on fire, we should not consider the problem of agriculture. But there is nothing to be gained by calling upon the people to make sacrifices greater than are necessary. The people are willing to make every sacrifice that will help the war effort in any way, but unnecessary sacrifices may prove to be a detriment to our efficiency. There is nothing to be gained by imposing unnecessary hardships upon the people. In fact such a procedure is almost criminal, because it may cause disunity in the ranks of labour and is likely to undermine the morale of the people.
I listened with a good deal of interest last week to the speech of the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Evans). I agree with what he said about the improvement of conditions in western Canada resulting from the increase in the price of live stock; nevertheless his speech may give a totally wrong impression of the conditions that really exist in the west. Throughout the west there is a large percentage of farmers who for various reasons have not been able to benefit by the increase in the price of live stock. In some cases this is due to a lack of pasture; in others to insufficient water, and in still others to lack of capital or credit with which to acquire live stock. We must remember that 72537-94
back in 1937, because of the drought, regulations were passed which caused the farmer to reduce his stock to two or three head per family in order that he might be able to acqujre feed from the department, and in large areas practically the entire stock was wiped out except for a few milk cows per family. Since then, unfortunately many of those farmers have not been in a position even to keep any increase in stock. They have had to sell their calves to get the wherewithal to live. Those farmers are not being benefited to any large extent by an increase in the price of live stock. Most people will also admit that the position of the grain grower in Canada as not being an enviable one.
But one of agriculture's greatest handicaps is that even where a farmer has a fair amount of stock he is only in a position to pay the interest on his accumulated debts. He is not, generally speaking, in a position to reduce the amount of his indebtedness. The hon. member for Maple Creek admitted that. If the farmers are not in a position to reduce the amount of their accumulated debt, what will be their position after the war, when there is a general fear that prices may be reduced? We hope they will not be; there is no reason why they should be, but from our experience of the past there is every reason to expect they will be. On the other hand, the farmer who is fortunate enough to be able to make a payment on his principal finds that he now has an additional burden of a tax of from thirty to forty per cent. In other words, the payment of his debt is being increased by thirty to forty per cent due to the income tax. The proviso that losses over the past two years may be offset against current income does not help the farmer who has heavy debts to meet because of losses incurred during the depression years.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How many farmers in the west are paying income tax?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member asks that question a year from now, the answer then would give a totally different impression from the answer to-day. The number of farmers in the west paying income tax to-day is small. Why? For the very simple reason that they are in the unenviable position of having a low income. In your returns you are allowed to deduct depreciation on equipment and interest on debt, but as I have already said, the debts of these farmers are so large that they have a very large interest payment to make and that will reduce the amount of income tax they have to pay. Nevertheless they will have to pay that interest in order to obtain the deduction in



The Budget-Mr. Quelch
income tax, and therefore the income they have left will be small.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will get as a deduction the amount they pay off on their mortgages, so that that will encourage them to pay off their mortgages.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The compulsory savings part of the tax is abolished if they make payments on their houses, but I am leaving that out as taxation. There is no deduction in the taxation, because that is compulsory savings. Taxation is taken away for good. If a part of it were to be returned as compulsory savings, there would not be the same objection.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is optimistic enough to believe that the farmers are going to be in the income tax class.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the farmer makes an income of over $660 he has to pay income tax.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. Under the new regulations, once the farmer gets over $660 he must pay income tax.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) may not pay it, but the rest of them do.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tragic accumulation of debts in western Canada is the inevitable outcome of federal policy during the past twelve years. In some cases the situation has undoubtedly been aggravated by drought. The situation cannot be blamed upon poor farming, nor can it be blamed upon the farmer's desire to avoid paying his obligations. While such cases may exist, they must be looked upon as the exception rather than the rule.
During the last war, from 1914 to 1919, it is true that generally speaking agriculture was prosperous, and I would especially commend that statement to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has tried to persuade the farmers of the west that they would not gain by a policy of inflation, but the farmers understand very well what the situation is. The farmers know far better than the minister himself that during a period of inflation they unquestionably do benefit-and I am not speaking in favour of inflation when I say that. But it has been the policy in Canada to try to persuade the farmers that they would lose as a result of inflation. The minister argues that the farmers would be no better off in a period of inflation, because although they would receive higher prices for what they have to sell, they would have to pay higher prices for what
[Mr. Quelch, 1
they have to buy. But the minister leaves out one very important factor. He misses the point that the majority of the farmers in western Canada are very heavily in debt, and the only way in which they will ever be able to pay those debts, unless action be taken to reduce them, is through a period of inflation. For instance, if a farmer has a debt of $1,000 and wheat is 50 cents a bushel, it takes two thousand bushels of wheat to pay off his debt, but if wheat is worth $1 a bushel it takes only one thousand bushels to pay off his debt. The minister leaves that entirely out of his argument.
It is also well to remember that the size of these debts was greatly increased during the years of deflation. The farmers were told then that they would have to accept world market prices for their products, and as a result of the disastrous prices of that period the debts of the farmers increased to a veiy great degree. Now, when the farmers might have a chance to gain, a ceiling is put on prices to prevent them from getting the benefit of higher prices for their products. If a floor had been placed under agricultural prices during the depression years there would be no kick. But why should the farmer be told in years of depression that he must accept world market prices, and then in years of inflation be told that he must take a price below the ceiling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because we are at war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then let us try to equalize the burden. The minister has taken steps to try to equalize the burden on other industries, where subsidies are being paid to make up the difference. We are still a long way off from making up the difference between the prices the farmer receives and what he should receive on a comparative basis with other industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Subsidies are being paid.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The mortgage companies have started actions for foreclosure in the west. They should be told that there is a war on and that the farmers cannot pay their debts because there is a war on. But the mortgage companies are demanding their pound of flesh. It would be a very good thing if they were told that there is a war on and that they can take no action to foreclose until after the war is over.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are the ones who need to know there is a war on.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister also stated
that inflation would be followed by deflation. But if the period of inflation lasted sufficiently long the farmer would be in a position

The Budget-Mr. Quelch
to reduce his debt and thereby be in a much better position to accept reduced prices. Prices after the last war fell from 1921 to 1924, but with rising prices from 1924 to 1929 agriculture, generally speaking, prospered, in spite of the deflation which the minister saj^s always follows a period of inflation. Agriculture prospered nevertheless, because the farmers had benefited so much during the period of high prices that they were in a better position to withstand the onslaught of the depression years.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not agree with that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By 192S or 1929 the majority of the farmers of western Canada could look forward to the future with a good deal of assurance, although prices at that time were still below a parity based on 1913-14. In 1928 many farmers were warned by their local bank managers that they should begin to curtail their expenditures. They were warned that they were on the eve of another depression. I know that because I happened to have had that experience. Therefore, apparently, even in 1928, one year before the depression started, the banks knew that a policy of curtailing loans was to be introduced. In 1929 many farmers who had been in the habit of going to the bank and getting a line of credit found, without any warning that line of credit cut off. The same thing applied to industries all over Canada. Consequently unemployment increased; the demand for goods decreased; the prices of primary products fell; and we were confronted with the vicious spiral of deflation. I do not think it is necessary for me to illustrate at any great length the depth to which prices fell in 1932. Wheat fell to nineteen and a half cents a bushel. In the city of Calgary it was selling at a lower price than sawdust. In that year I shipped 200 dressed turkeys, prime birds, which netted me five cents a pound dressed. Oats went down to four cents a bushel; 200-pound dressed hogs fetched five dollars apiece. Was it any wonder that the farmers went heavily into debt during that period? They continually asked that a floor should be placed under prices; but no action was taken, and it is only natural that they should deplore that to-day, when they have a chance to recover some of the losses incurred in those years, a ceiling should be placed on prices to make that impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was a floor under
wheat.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was no floor under wheat in 1932. It dropped to nineteen and a half cents a bushel. If there was any floor it 72537-94}
must have been a rotten one, because they went through it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But there was a floor under wheat in 1935.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, in 1935 there was,
but that was after five years of low prices. How could any industry produce for five years at less than the cost of production without going into debt unless it had big reserves to fall back upon; and agriculture did not have any reserves.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some agriculturists weathered the storm. Why not others?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. I am always having the example of these men held up to me.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have on one side of the road a farmer who is bankrupt, and on the other side a farmer who is prosperous.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Exactly.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the difference?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The farmer himself.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would say that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it will be found that the prosperous farmer has had access to some other source of income.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does not the ability of the farmer himself enter into the question of his own prosperity, as it does in industry?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly. But I noticed during the depression that the concerns which went under first were very often those which were held up as examples of efficiency. Take the great Campbell farms in the United States, which were publicized in the press year after year as the last word in efficient administration. They went bankrupt, because they could not carry on below a certain price. Many farmers could continue only by getting their wives and young children to do work which should not be required of them. But that is not done in industry. You do not see men like Gordon and Flavelle getting their wives to keep books and so on without pay.
In this ten-year period from 1929 to 1939 the returns for agricultural products, with few exceptions, were considerably below costs of production. No attempt was made to maintain a parity price based upon the year 1926, nor was any attempt made to reduce prices of farm machinery to the farmer, in spite of the fact that a committee of this house found that prices of farm machinery were excessive. Furthermore, according to figures presented to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations by the government of Manitoba, the policy of appreciating the
The Budget-Mr. Quelch

Canadian dollar twenty per cent above the pound sterling, while Australia depreciated its currency twenty-five per cent below the pound sterling, cost the farmers of western Canada from 1931 to 1936 $47,000,000 a year on an average. In addition, according to the same brief, the tariff cost the farmers of western Canada during the same period $32,000,000 a year, making the total cost the farmers should not have had to bear $79,000,000 a year over that six-year period.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I assert that it is the responsibility of the federal government to introduce without delay measures to bring about security of tenure to the farmer for the duration of the war and as long afterwards as the present restrictions remain in force, and also an equitable adjustment of all farm debts at a low rate of interest, based upon ability to pay. I think the need of such action is demonstrated by figures quoted in 17. F. C. Information, issue of February, 1943, page one, which states:
The most recent figure available on farm debts in Saskatchewan is $630,000,000 or $21 debt average on the 30,000,000 acres cultivated in this province. It is estimated that the average debt on the higher quality wheat land is $30 per cultivated acre. It should be remembered that much of this land operates the practice of summer-fallowing one-half of the land each year, consequently each crop acre in such circumstances carries a debt responsibility of $60 per acre, requiring $4.20 to satisfy interest obligation.
The present pressure from the various creditor classes is having a detrimental effect on western agriculture. Many farmers are being compelled to sell immature stock; for instance, calves. There should be a law prohibiting the sale of many calves and yearlings which are now sold only because the farmers are compelled to do so in order to meet their obligations. That kind of thing is not helping the war effort. To-day many farmers are disposing of breeding stock which should not be sold, and which they are selling only because they are obliged to do so, either by their creditors or through force of circumstances.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has announced for this year an ambitious programme for agriculture. The minister admits that it will not be easy to put that programme into effect. Many farmers are already working to the limit of their endurance. However, there are many steps which the government could take to ease the burdens of agriculture. First, place the farmer on a par with labour in so far as ceilings are concerned; that is, put these ceilings at the highest level of prices from 1926 to 1940. According to Leonard D. Nesbitt, as quoted at

page 4 of 17. F. C. Information, if this were done prices of grains could be approximately at these levels.
Per bushel
Wheat	 $1.60
Oats	69
Barley	90
Rye	 1.35
Flax	 3.00

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would there not be an increased surplus of commodities we already have?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, because there is a quota delivery.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who will pay for something he does not want?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a quota delivery, and farmers will be able to build up in their own granaries a slight reserve beyond the quota to take care of bad years.
Then a floor should be placed under agricultural prices for at least three years after the war. That floor should be based upon parity prices of 1926-29. Before leaving the question of price I should like to refer briefly to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture. Speaking in this house on February 9, he emphasized the need for building up large reserves to take care of the war-torn countries after the war. He mentioned that grain could probably be more easily stored than any other commodity. Government policy to-day is to take delivery of an amount equal to the year's sales. The quota system has been established, and generally speaking it works well. But the production of that quota must be looked upon as part of the war effort, for it is realized to be desirable to maintain this reserve in order to take care of the war-torn areas after the war. Therefore farmers are entitled to a parity price for that quota as it is delivered, looking upon it as part of the war effort. They are entitled to the same consideration as every other industry operating during the war.
The minister admits that the price received by the farmer to-day for grain is considerably below a parity based upon 1926-29. The minister states that the price of wheat is 54-5 cents below parity. On oats it is 9 cents below; on barley, 11-2 cents below, and on rye, 38-5 cents below. One may well ask why the farmers should be discriminated against in that way. I maintain they are entitled to a ceiling based on the highest price of 1926 to 1940.
But below that ceiling there should be a floor based on parity of 1926-29. The Minister of Agriculture points out that present prices are still far below that floor.

The Budget-Mr. McNevin
The minister attempts to defend that price by saying that the government is short of funds for the purpose of establishing a floor. If that statement is tme it shows that the government have not maintained the policy that they said at the beginning of the war would be maintained. Both the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister stated' that no financial restriction would be allowed to interfere with the efficiency of our war effort. But whenever you ask any body of people to produce below cost of production you are destroying the efficiency of that organization. It is compelling farmers to sell stock which in the interest of the nation should not be sold.
Apparently the government are afraid that higher prices will cause inflation. If the government are really afraid that an increase in prices to agriculture wmuld cause inflation, I make this suggestion: let the government make up the difference between the present price of grain and the parity price by an issue of war savings certificates to the farmers. The minister says this would cause an increase in debt. However, the government to-day is incurring debt to stabilize other prices. Why should the grain grower be the one exception to that rule? I maintain that the farmers are entitled to be allowed a share in the national war debt. The minister reiterates that it is debt to ourselves. Then I say there should be a fairer distribution of that debt. We must make it possible to-day for the farmer, generally speaking, to buy an equal share of bonds or war savings certificates along with other people.
In order that agriculture may in the future play its full part in this war effort, I hope the government will give greater consideration to a number of the points I have raised to-day.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like at the outset of my remarks to offer a few suggestions which in my opinion would facilitate the passing of legislation, the granting of supply and the provision of ways and means in this House of Commons. I am prompted to offer these suggestions by reason of the protracted discussion which has taken place on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and again in the budget debate.
I am not unmindful of the fact that there should be in a country like Canada at least one occasion in each parliamentary session wherein there would be the fullest opportunity to discuss the most extended range of questions, because we are a difficult country to govern, since we have far-flung and widely separated areas where the environment and the industry and the lives of the people differ
greatly from those in other sections of the country. I am also not unmindful of the fact that you cannot take any particular country's parliament or legislative assembly as a pattern and expect to fit it to some other country, because conditions prevailing in each and every country, influence the actions and conduct of the parliaments or legislative assemblies of the different countries.
Looking over the debates on the address in reply in the British House of Commons in the four war sessions, I find the length of time occupied in each year was as follows: In the session of 1939-40, six days; in the session of 1940-41. six days; in the session of 1941-42, eight days and in the session of 1942-43, eleven days. Of course they usually start in the fall, earlier than we do. That completes the record for those four years.
In offering these suggestions I do not wish to make it appear that there should be any infringement upon the rights and privileges of lion, members or any impairment of the ability of our legislative institutions successfully and fully to discharge their duty to the people of Canada, However, I think every hon. member will agree that in the lengthy debate on the address in reply this year and in this budget debate considerable duplication, and repetition have occurred, which do not promote efficiency in any legislative body.
Therefore the first suggestion I have to offer is that we adopt a principle that has long been in use in the British House of Commons. It is usually referred to as allocation of time. I have gone back to the session of 1881 in the British House of Commons, when a resolution was passed granting authority to control, guide or direct the passage of legislation by what they termed the allocation of time. I should like to read from pages 57 and 58 of the journals of the British House of Commons for February 3 and 4. 1881:
Then the main question, so amended, being put-[DOT]
This has to do with the business of the house, under the heading of "urgency."
-resolved, that if upon notice given a motion be made by a minister of the crown that the state of public business is urgent, upon which motion such minister shall declare in his place that any bill, motion or other question then before the house is urgent and that it is of importance to the public interest that the same should be proceeded with without delay, the Speaker shall forthwith put the question, no debate, amendment, or adjournment being allowed; and if, on the voices being given he shall wdthout doubt perceive that the "noes"
The Budget-Mr. McNevin

have it, his decision shall not be challenged, but, if otherwise, a division may be forthwith taken, and if the question be resolved in the affirmative by a majority of not less than three to one, in a house of not less than three hundred members, the powers of the house for the regulation of its business upon the several stages of bills, and upon motions and all other matters, shall be and remain with the Speaker, for the purpose of proceeding with such bill, motion, or other question, until the Speaker shall declare that the state of public business is no longer urgent, or until the house shall so determine, upon a motion which, after notice given, may be made by any member, put without amendment, adjournment, or debate, and decided by a majority.
This is followed by this sentence:
Mr. Gladstone, the first lord of the treasury having declared in his place that the bill for the protection of persons and property (Ireland) now before the house is urgent and that it is of importance to the public interest that the same should be proceeded with without delay; resolved that the state of public business is urgent.
Then they' went on with the bill. Not being a member of the legal profession, I do not intend to enter into an analysis of the technicalities of this question, but I should like to lay down one or two broad principles upon which it might be considered. Before doing so, however, I wish to give a further quotation having regard to a definite bill, taken from the journals of the British house for 1904 at pages 291 and 294, under the heading, "Procedure on the Licensing Bill." I read first from page 291:
That the proceedings in committee and on report of the licensing bill shall be brought to a conclusion in the manner hereinafter mentioned on six allotted days:-
(a)	The proceedings in committee on clause
1	on the first allotted day;
(b)	The proceedings in committee on clauses
2	and 3 on the second allotted day;
(c)	The proceedings in committee on clause 4 on the third allotted day;
(d)	The proceedings in committee on the remaining clauses of the bill, and on any new government clauses, and on schedules and any new government schedules, and any other proceedings necessary to bring the committee stage to a conclusion, on the fourth allotted day;
(e)	The proceedings on report on any new clauses and on amendments to clauses 1, 2, and
3	of that bill, be brought to a conclusion on the fifth allotted day; and
(f)	The proceedings on report be concluded on the sixth allotted day.
After this order comes into operation, any day shall be considered an allotted day for the purposes of this order on which the licensing bill is put down as the first order of the day.
At eleven p.m. on the said allotted days or, if the day is a Friday, at 4.30 p.m., the Chairman or Speaker shall put forthwith the question or questions on any amendment or motion already proposed from the Chair, and shall next proceed successively to put forthwith the 
question on any amendments moved by the government of which notice has been given (but no other amendments), and on every question necessary to dispose of the allotted business to be concluded on the allotted day.
Then, further, on page 294, under the heading "Licensing Bill (first allotted day)":
The house, according to order, resolved itself into a committee on the licensing bill.
I may not be entirely correct in my assumptions, but in my opinion under that resolution there is vested in the Speaker of the British House of Commons the right to allocate certain specific time, a day, part of a day, or a number of days, for the consideration of any specific bill or measure. Further, with regard to the allocation of time, I find the following at pages 348, 349 and 350 of May's Parliamentary Practice:
The temporary provision made by the urgency resolutions of sessions 1881 and 1882 for the consideration of important bills has been mentioned on page 332, and some description must now be given of the arrangements that have been made in subsequent sessions to ensure the completion of various stages of bills and other business. Orders of the house have prescribed the times at which and the proceedings by which the remaining part or the whole of the committee stage, the report stage, the committee and report stages, the report stage and third reading, the committee and report stages and third reading and the second reading and subsequent stages of a bill should be disposed of.
Then, with respect to ways and means I have just a short quotation which I think has also some bearing on the question, from page 883 of the same volume:
As soon as the committee of supply has been appointed and estimates have been presented, the business of supply shall, until disposed of, be the first order of the day on Thursday, unless the house otherwise order on the motion of a minister of the crown, moved at the commencement of public business, to be decided without amendment or debate.
(2)	Not more than twenty days, being days before the fifth of August, shall be allotted for the consideration of the annual estimates for the army, navy, air force, and civil services, including votes on account. The days allotted shall not include any day on which the question has to be put that the Speaker do leave the chair, or any day on which the business of supply does not stand as first order.
(3)	Provided that the days occupied by the consideration of estimates supplementary to those of a previous session or of any vote of credit, or of votes for supplementary or additional estimates presented by the government for war expenditure, or for any new- service not included in the ordinary estimates for the year, shall not be included in the computation of the twenty days aforesaid.
(4)	Provided also that on motion made after notice, to be decided without amendment or debate, additional time, not exceeding three days, may be allotted for the purposes aforesaid, either before or after the 5th of August.

The Budget-Mr. McNevin
(5)	On a day bo allotted, no business other than the business of supply shall be taken before eleven, and no business in committee or proceedings on report of supply shall be taken after eleven, whether a general order exempting business from interruption under the standing order (sittings of the house) is in force or not, unless the house otherwise order on the motion of a minister of the crown, moved at the commencement of public business, to be decided without amendment or debate.
Paragraphs 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 bear on this point, but I shall not deal further with this aspect of the situation.
Consideration might be given, particularly in war time, to adding a standing order to our standing orders providing for an allocation of time. I wish further to supplement what I have said by referring to the procedure in the South African house of assembly. I find this at page 4, volume 1, of their standing orders:
(11): Mr. Speaker shall report to the house the governor gem1 rat's speech, and there shall be no debate on such report.
The South African parliament is the youngest in the British commonwealth of nations, and I assume they have profited from the mistakes made by senior parliaments.

May I now say a word respecting post-war problems, and I shall turn first to that of employment because it has a bearing on rural problems. I do not believe there is any single item offering greater opportunity for employment than an endeavour to extend electrical services to as many as possible of the rural residents throughout Canada. The construction of transmission lines, and the provision of the necessary metals and equipment would require a great amount of industrial employment. I am sure the house will agree with me when I say there is no class of citizen in Canada more entitled to the benefit of laboursaving devices than farm people generally, and particularly farm women.
We have in Canada at the present time a turbine installation amounting to 9,225,000 horse-power. There is available within reasonable distance of the more densely populated areas of this country an additional three to four million horse-power. It is estimated that the total available power resources at the present time amount to 51,000,000 horse-power,
The Budget-Mr. McNevin

but approximately three-quarters of this is too far away to be of much use. There has been considerable development in order to provide the additional power needed for our war industries, so that I do not think the matter of additional installations in the post-war period will create any problem. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has referred to one of our great industries which uses in the neighbourhood of 2,000,000 horsepower, between a fifth or a sixth of the entire available electrical energy. It is unlikely that after the war we shall be able to find immediate use for the aluminum, the manufacture of which is now consuming such large quantities of power. Therefore large blocks of power will be available for distribution, at least some in the manner I have outlined.
There are other items which might be considered. I was considerably interested in the report made to the British house by Sir William Beveridge and in the report presented to this House of Commons dealing with social reconstruction. In the consideration of our post-war problems there is one thing that should not be overlooked. The economic committee of the League of Nations and the international institute of agriculture, assisted by experts from almost every country in the world, spent several months in an intensive and exhaustive investigation into the causes of the depression. They came to the conclusion that the depression in agricultural prices was at the root of the general problem.
No matter how great a social programme may be constituted in this parliament or in the parliaments of other democratic countries, it cannot be maintained unless we keep foremost in our mind the fact that depressed prices of farm products were at the root of the last depression. Unless international thought is given to preventing these prices from going down to the point reached in the last depression, it will be impossible to maintain our social plans at the point indicated by such legislation. Unless prices of agricultural products are kept up to a reasonable level, the success of such legislation will be impossible.
I have but a few minutes longer, and in the time at my disposal I should like to refer to the one matter which is more important than any of the others coming up for consideration in this house. I refer to the prosecution of the war. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has now enrolled in the Canadian army approximately 450,000 persons. Our first and greatest tribute must go to the loyal and courageous citizens who have volunteered for service in the army in such large numbers. 
Some tribute should also be paid to the minister and to those who have preceded him in that office for the guidance, direction and leadership they have given to the Canadian army.
Approximately 55,000 persons have been enrolled for service under the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. The persons in this service have had more action to date than those men who have enlisted in our army, and, I am sure, are giving a splendid account of themselves on the seven seas. These gallant young men and women should receive the highest tribute, not only from the Canadian people but from this parliament. The present Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) is the first minister who has served in this capacity, and he also is deserving of commendation for the guidance, direction and leadership he has given as chief of this branch of our Canadian forces.
Just a word about the air force. We have in the Royal Canadian Air Force approximately 200,000 persons who have enlisted for active service anywhere. The same tribute should be paid to these men and women. They represent a highly skilled and highly trained section of our population. The very nature of their work is such as to make this high training almost essential. We owe a debt of gratitude to the personnel of our air force, and this debt is all the greater because to date they have suffered greater casualties than any of the other services. I am not sure as to the naval service, but I believe this is true'as far as the army is concerned. The people of Canada will, I am certain, join with this parliament in paying a tribute to the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), who has the responsibility of supervising this most essential branch of our armed forces.
I have just one more thought, namely, in relation to the post-war period when victory is won and our forces return. I think what is uppermost in the minds of most of these young men and young women is this thought: What am I coming back to? So that I think the least we can do is to provide them with what might be termed security. They must be protected from the scourge of unemployment; they must be protected from the ravages of disease; they must be provided with medical services and hospitalization, which latter is already receiving the consideration of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) ; and they must also be provided with an opportunity to earn a decent standard of living for themselves, or for themselves and their wives arid families, as the case may be.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I consider it a compliment to myself that Mr. Deputy Speaker has made his first official appearance this evening. I also regard it as a personal compliment that, after I had prepared an excellent speech, expecting to make it last Friday, Mr. Churchill, the great Prime Minister of Great Britain, unfortunately made it on Sunday. So that I am rather embarrassed. I understand also that to-day a certain "other place" is having a meeting in opposition to mine.
We have heard a great many speeches in this debate. Everything under the sun has been discussed, including imaginary battles on the St. Lawrence and isolationism; we have even heard of a tunnel built out of one province-I suppose, for no other reason than that the inhabitants can move into British Columbia any time at all. For that reason I favour it.
I only wish that in some way we could have the privilege which a certain provincial member had, of writing our speeches a few days ahead and handing it to the newspapers, particularly those of our own riding, to be printed in full, and without the mistakes which I may possibly be supposed to make, although I do not intend to make any.
I am more or less on the spot this evening. I have had to follow the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), who, by the way, paid me the honour of visiting my riding. They deliberately sent a young man into the constituency of Fraser Valley as representing their party, because it takes an aggressive and progressive young man to find a Tory remaining in that riding.
I listened with a great deal of pleasure to wha,t in my opinion is the most all-embracing budget ever delivered, and which was presented by the man whom I regard as the most competent Minister of Finance we have ever had. Next to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has the most difficult problem of any member of the government. I am sorry that the finance minister is not present to hear the compliments I am paying him, but of course I shall see that he gets a copy of my speech to-morrow. Holding, as he does, this most difficult position, he has made an excellent job in his new budget. He has taxed nearly everyone in the dominion, as fairly as any man can place taxation. I am sorry to have to say that in some instances I fear he has lost
sight of the principle of "ability to pay", but we must give him credit for spreading taxes throughout the nation, and restricting to a very large extent the amassing of fortunes through excessive war profits.
I would, however, make a couple of suggestions. I urge the minister to give every consideration to what is known as the Ruml plan. Strange as it may seem, this recommendation is not coming in my riding from what might be called the privileged class. Every labour organization we have in the riding has made that request. I also think that further consideration should be given to any taxation which may be imposed upon cooperatives. I am sorry the minister is not in his seat at the moment. I am one of those, I suppose, who got more or less of a verbal spanking yesterday for saying what was, in the opinion of some, our idea of improvements and mistakes that have been made; although I do not share in all these opinions. Let there be no misunderstanding. I will describe, with the assistance of an able authority, what I think of Donald Gordon, the present leader-I suppose I should call him-of the wartime prices and trade board. I quote from Hansard, at page 1427:
I want to say now that I have never met a man with greater honesty or integrity, with greater moral courage, with greater capacity for straight clear thinking, with greater capacity for hard, nerve-wracking work, with greater capacity for decision or with more unselfish devotion to duty.
I have repeated the words of the Minister of Finance, who thought that some of us had criticized in a personal way Donald Gordon. I would add that I also think he is a very fine gentleman, and I might inform hon. members that there is no man with whom one can spend a more enjoyable evening in a personal way. I watched him come up the corridor to-day at six o'clock and realized that he must have heard that Cruickshank would speak about him to-night.
I wish to make my point clear in connection with criticism of the wartime prices and trade board, because that is what I shall principally speak about to-night. I do not object to the verbal spanking which I assumed I, as representing the Fraser valley, was getting with the rest, but my constituents sent me here to express their views to the best of my ability.
Although I did not agree with everything said by the leader of the opposition in what I thought was an excellent speech, I am in agreement with him when he said that there is nobody in Canada but wants to prevent inflation. He also pointed out-I do not know

I must admit that I cannot conceive of anything capable of holding back the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth); he always comes through.
Just for a moment I wish to refer to the agricultural policy of the Progressive Conservative party. You know, Mr. Speaker, I am beginning to get a little muddled as to the right name of that party, though I always want

The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank
to be courteous and to describe it correctly. The other day, when I read .the newspaper, I did not know whether it should be called the Progressive Conservative party or the progressive "curling party". I should like to quote what St. James street has to say about our policy after the war, and St. James street cannot possibly be taken to represent either the Liberal party or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group. This quotation is from a publication called Trend, and I had better give the address as well. I do not know whether this is the home of the famous committee of 200, but the address is 291 St. James street, and this is what it says:
The secondary industries of Canada cannot do the job if the Canadian markets for their products are subject to free competition from the products of Great Britain, the United States . . .
Then a little further on:
If the domestic markets in Canada are to be denied to them, how can they hope to survive after the close of the war?
Then there is another paragraph, which I think is very apropos, following the speech of the financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party:
Is it not high time that those who direct Canadian industries should consider which trade and fiscal policies shall prevail in Canada after the war, and take a lively interest in their preparation and development?
In other words, according to St. James street big business must prepare at once to see to it that our tariffs are raised not against farm produce but rather against that which is necessary in order to produce it, such as farm machinery.
I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not in his seat at the moment, because it is many years since I have been so severely spanked, and I rather enjoyed it. I never got enough of it at school, I am told, though it seemed to me I got plenty. I wish to say to the minister that I resent being told that I cannot criticize the composition of some of these boards. I believe there are fifty-seven lawyers in this House of Commons; and I am willing to sit down now for ten minutes if one of those lawyers will rise in his place and say he would permit a dairy farmer to put a ceiling on the prices they may charge. That is the whole point; that is our whole argument when we insist that a practical agriculturist should set the ceilings on farm prices. Would it be reasonable to have a doctor setting the price of newsprint?
