speechtext: Your party does not listen to you.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, my party already has the advantage of being composed of intelligent men, and I am trying to convert some of the rest of the hon. members. When I was a small boy I was asked why I was Liberal, if it was simply because my father was Liberal. I replied, "Frankly, yes," and any other small boy would say the same thing. But I would add that as soon as I was old enough to think for myself I naturally became a Liberal, because no one who does any thinking would be anything else, under the old two-party system.
I should now like to say a word in connection with the Pacific coast problem, particularly as it concerns British Columbia. Some of our hon. friends in the far comer to my left have advocated that we should not have moved the Japanese from the coast and in fact should move them back. They lose sight of the fact that at the present time Japan controls about one-quarter of the population of the entire world, and twice as many natural resources as the entire United States. Those hon. members must remember that we have not won this war as yet; that according to our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Prime Minister of Great Britain we still have a long, hard battle ahead of us before we defeat Hitler, and then we have to turn round and defeat Japan. Naturally we are not admitting any doubt as to the ultimate result, but we are facing that problem. Nevertheless those people object to moving the Japanese out of British Columbia purely for defence reasons, and want us to take them back. I do not know why they want us to have the Japanese back, unless they think the Japanese should be given the vote in British Columbia, but I want to warn those people that Japan will be a tough nut to crack, and that British Columbia will be a tough nut to crack when the Japanese peace terms are drawn up, as far as bringing back the Japanese is concerned.
I wish to pay my respects to one hon. member from Saskatchewan. I have heard many hon. members from that province say in this house that they must be paid a bonus for not producing wheat. The other evening I listened with a great deal of interest to another hon. member repeating what we have been saying for two years, that when peace comes we cannot have too much wheat on hand. But the most charming speech of all was when another hon. member from Saskatchewan tried to claim that his province leads all others in social legislation. Coming from British Columbia, I could not quite take that. Even my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party will admit that British Columbia leads all the provinces in

The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank
social legislation, most of which was brought in when our present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) was a member of the provincial government, which speaks well for the social security we may get under this federal government. Ours was the first province to have the eight-hour day, and the minimum wage. Ours is the province paying the highest benefits to widows and mothers.
I should like to make it perfectly clear that my riding is absolutely in favour of any policy that will assist in preventing inflation, and we think we have demonstrated that. But we say to the minister, in all seriousness, as was said this afternoon, that in our opinion the best way to avoid upsetting the apple cart as far as inflation is concerned is to see.to it that the farmer is paid a reasonable return for what he produces, and he is not getting that to-day. If you do not want to have a feeling all across Canada which might upset the whole principle, agriculture must be treated better than it is being treated to-day. There is an hon. gentleman who comes from Ontario, and there is no more highly respected or better known member of this House of Commons. His father was born in Canada and is now eighty years of age, and while the hon. member is attending his duties in the House of Commons at Ottawa his father must milk the cows night and morning. In my opinion that is not good enough, and it is because we do not receive proper prices for farm products.
I wish to pay my respects to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, under whose department, I understand, the matter to which I now wish to refer comes. I do not think we can possibly put rehabilitation or reconstruction on an all-cmbracing scale into effect until after the war, and even then we can do so only in conjunction with the allied nations. I do not think it is feasible to do so until the end of the war, no matter what party is in power. This is something which in my opinion must be done internationally. But we may put a scheme of health insurance into effect. If we are sincere in our talk about social security, we will pass the enabling legislation before parliament prorogues or adjourns.
There is one further point to which we must give more attention. There reached me today from the secretary of the Union of British Columbia Municipalities a letter which should have appeal for every hon. member, particularly those from British Columbia. This organization represents eighty-five per cent of the people in that province. The letter deals with the treatment accorded our discharged
men from this war. I understand we give a man $27 to re-outfit himself with clothing, if he has served for six months, and $17 if he has served for less than six months. Those are the figures I have been given. The letter states that the amount is $20. This matter is sei'ious because a letter is enclosed which is being circularized throughout British Columbia. It deals with a matter which I say we must adjust, if we are sincere in our statements about social security. The letter is being circularized by the Salvation Army, one of the finest organizations in the land, either in this war or at the time of the last one. I shall not quote all of the letter, but I say the matter is serious enough for the minister's consideration, especially when it comes from an organization such as the Salvation Army. One paragraph of the circular letter reads:
Also, there is an increasing demand upon us for clothing to outfit discharged soldiers and return them to civilian life. The poor we still have with us, and many destitute families.
That is not a good enough condition, in this present day and age. We have nothing in this parliament to be proud of, and the Liberal government has nothing to be proud of if such a condition does exist; and in view of a letter such as this, coming from such a reputable organization, one must conclude that it does, exist.
I give the Minister of Finance and his board full credit. We know we do not have to pay the prices for boots and shoes that we had to pay after the last war. If I remember correctly, I received $35 to outfit myself when I came back, and my first pair of boots cost me $15, or almost half of the amount I received. Surely it is not the intention of the government to permit a condition to exist under which the Salvation Army or any other organization, must appeal to charity to outfit the men and women who are being discharged from our armed services.
Mr. Speaker, according to the clock I still have three and three-quarter minutes left to me. However, after listening (o the speeches of hon. members I have concluded that one gets tired of listening. Mr. Churchill spoke for only forty-five minutes, and he said more in three minutes than hon. members on this side of the house, including myself, could say in four days. And when I speak for myself I believe I can speak for all hon. members in the house. I have listened to and read their speeches, and I believe I am correct in what I say.
I do wish to impress upon the Department of Finance that any criticism we. may make is not made with the intention of breaking the system of war-time price levels. I

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
say, as did the leader of the opposition today, that the people in my constituency, as they have in the past, will carry their full share of the next victory loan. We will do what we have done in the past-something which has not been done by part of the rest of Canada-namely, carry more than our share of voluntary enlistments.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although it is the duty of an opposition to offer deserved criticism and to make constructive suggestions, it seems to me it is only fair to recall that when in the fall of 1939 Canada declared war we were in no respect prepared for it. We had only a small army, woefully lacking in equipment. Our navy and our air force were negligible. We had no factories producing arms and ammunition, no shipyards building war ships, no factories building war planes.
To-day the picture has changed. We have an army, a navy and an air force. We have a fighting navy and a fighting air force of which we may be proud. They are doing their full share in the battles of the allied nations. Our army, with the exception of those poor fellows who were sent to Hong Kong and Dieppe, has seen no fighting. It is still in training in England, and here at home in Canada. But when the time comes for the Canadian army to go into battle, they can be depended upon to do their duty. We are turning out supplies ample for our own forces, and contributing quantities of armaments and food for our allies. That, in view of our small population, compared with the populations in allied countries, and in view of the limited wealth of the average Canadian, is an accomplishment of which I say we may well be proud.
Mistakes have been made, and doubtless are being made. In a country unprepared, unequipped and untrained for war, that was inevitable. However, little valid excuse can be offered for the unsatisfactory allocation or regimentation of Canada's man-power to cope with war-time needs. We are faced with a shortage of man-power in the lumber woods, in the sawmills and on the farms. We have a shortage of food produced by the farms because those farms have been stripped of man-power, the power they need and must have if they are to produce. Prices of farm products have been kept so low' by the government that farmers are unable to produce the needed foods. There is a shortage of beef and a shortage of butter. Why? Because beef cattle from Canada have been shipped in such quantities to foreign markets. On account of the shortage of farm labour, dairy farmers have been forced to send their milking herds 
to the slaughter houses. One has only to visit the farms in the Fraser Valley, that portion of Canada from which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) who just preceded me comes, to learn the plight of the farmers there. There a dairy farmer gets for 100 pounds of Jersey milk, containing 4-07 pounds of butter fat-wonderfully rich milk- the paltry sum of SI.45. The consumer in Vancouver pays thirteen cents a quart for that milk, and for the 100 pounds he will pay $5.72. That represents a spread of S4.27 between the price received by the farmer and the amount paid by the consumer. That is too much. The farmer should get more and the middleman less.
Some hon. members, including some of the ministers, have been prone to boast of Canada's accomplishments in this war, compared with those of the last one. In the first three years of the last war Canada's army had made a fighting record which w7ill never die. Some hon. members and some of the ministers w'ere in that war. They know what they went through and what was accomplished in the field of battle. In this war Canada's army has still to make a record to equal that of the old Canadian expeditionary force. That Canada's army, still in training in England in this third year of the wrar, wTill make its record w'hen the time comes, I have not the slightest doubt.
When comparing Canada's production of war materials in this war with those of the last war the fact that Canada's population has materially increased in the interval, and that Canada's manufacturing industries have materially increased should not be lost sight of. The last great war was Canada's first experience in wrar. It was a new experience, and it was then that wre learned about war. When Canada declared war in 1939 we had the experience of the last war to guide us; we had learned how to go about war and war production. Canada's record in the last war was good, but in this war it is better in some respects and it should be better.
We see on posters and billboards the expression: "We are all in the front line." That was said by our king when speaking to the people of England, and it has been picked up here in Canada far from the front line and used to encourage enlistments and subscriptions to government loans. Let me give a brief description of what Britain had to face in the front line, after the evacuation of Dunkirk. Prime Minister Churchill disclosed that although Germany had thousands of tanks, Britain had fewer than one hundred, all of a type not able to stand up against German anti-tank guns. In July, 1940, Great Britain had only one fully equipped army division.

The Budget-Mr. Blade (Yukon)
In September, 1940, the Royal Air Force had only five fighters in reserve. Figures given in the publication Front Line show that in 1940 and 1941 no fewer than 43,667 civilians were killed in England and 50,387 were hospitalized as a result of air assaults.
In the first of the three large air attacks on London, that of July 16, 1941, 450 nazi bombers killed 1,000 persons and wounded as many more. Three nights later more than a thousand were killed. In the big attack on London on May 10, 1941, a total of 1,436 were killed and 1,792 injured by bombs from 500 hun planes. Attacks began on London in May, 1940. Every night for the first month they raided, and 5,730 were killed and 10,000 wounded. In September, 1940, the destruction of homes in Great Britain amounted to 40,000 to 50,000 weekly. By May, 1941, these figures had grown to 1,151,000 homes destroyed and
375,000	Londoners made homeless. That was being in the front line.
These figures give some idea of the stamina of the British people. They stood up against that alone and fought it out single-handed. None of her allies set up a second front to lessen the attacks on Great Britain. Russia did not come into the war until attacked' by Germany. The United States of America did not fight until attacked by Japan. Fortunately for the British commonwealth of nations those attacks were made, and Britain now has those grand allies, Russia and the United States, fighting by her side against the common enemies, Germany, Italy and Japan.
Recently some members of this house protested against some province or municipality in Canada barring Japanese children from its public schools. Before the war, in some of the schools of Vancouver a white child was a curiosity; the pupils were practically all Japanese. As I see it, that prohibition is just and right. Canada has no moral or other obligation to educate the children of her enemy. Before the war, the small fruit growing industry in the Fraser valley was practically a Japanese monopoly; they had literally frozen out the white man. Now that the Japs are gone, the white men are doing the growing. The fruit is being produced, and the Japs are not missed. We do not need them.	[DOT]
Before this war, the fishing on the coast of British Columbia was also practically a Japanese monopoly. They have been sent away, and white Canadian fishermen are catching the fish and supplying the markets. We can get along without the Japanese fishermen. All of the Japs are our enemies. If they are to be trusted, why have they
been evacuated from the coast areas? They were evacuated because we could not trust them. They were not evacuated for their own safety, they were evacuated for our safety from them. I say: feed them, house them, if necessary clothe them, but watch them and guard them until the time comes to deport them all from the continent of North America.
Speaking in this house as long ago as May 8, 1922, twenty-one years ago, along with other hon. members I advocated the expropriation of Japanese property in Canada at fair prices and their deportation from the country. Then we were not at war with Japan. To-day we are at war with Japan. They have attacked Canada, Australia and the United States. Therefore, I do not say, expropriate; I say, confiscate their property. It is enemy property; confiscate it and send them back whence they and their ancestors came. They are a menace to this country; there is no room for them on this continent.
During the past year we have heard much about the building of the Alaska highway. I have seen some of it built and have travelled over stretches of it. Canadians must not forget that it is being built and will be maintained throughout the war by the United States with United States money. The United States consider transportation through Canada to Alaska of sufficient importance to warrant them in building and financing the project. The Alaska highway is a good job, well done, but it is not a miracle. The route traverses no unexplored country. The builders had unlimited numbers of men, thousands of them, and unlimited quantities of the most up-to-date road building machinery known to man. They had all the money they required, and more. They had priorities on everything, on men and materials. To say that it was a bigger job than the building of the Panama canal is drawing a long bow. In our admiration for that project we should not lose sight of another project, a Canadian project known to comparatively few of the people of this country.
About forty years ago the government of Canada built a road in the Yukon over just such country as the Alaska highway traverses, from White Horse to Dawson. That road, about one-fifth the length of the Alaska highway, was built in one summer with a crew of not more than three hundred men, equipped not with power shovels, bull-dozers and giant graders but with ploughs drawn by horses and men equipped with picks and shovels. And very little money was available. By fall

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
the road was open for use. It was opened without the fanfare of trumpets, without any severing of ribbons with golden scissors. Like the Alaska highway, it was a good job well done. Until the advent of aeroplane transportation it was the only avenue in and out of the Yukon in the winter time. Thousands of tons of freight have been hauled over it, and thousands of people have made use of 'it. It is still in use.
I have no desire to belittle or make light of the task Qf building the Alaska highway. It is a splendid accomplishment, worthy of our admiration, worthy of the name "Alaska highway". It should not have to bear that disgustingly suggestive name of "Alcan highway". I realize that the word "Alcan" was intended by its inventors to make use of the first two letters in the word "Alaska" and the first three letters in "Canada". I am sure Canadians and, I hope, United States citizens as well dislike that ugly nickname and prefer to call that grand project what it is, a highway to Alaska, the Alaska highway. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced that by agreement between Canada and the United States that road was to be built, knowing that country as I do and what it meant to Canada, I hastened to suggest to the parks branch of the Department of Mines and Resources, to the game commission of British Columbia, and to the government of Yukon, that efficient and prompt measures should be taken for the protection of game along the Canadian section of that highway. I am glad to know and to be able to tell the house that, at the instance of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), the government of Canada has created a national park and game reserve in that great area southwest of the Alaska highway. It is an area of 10,130 square miles, a veritable game paradise, a country too precious to be desecrated or destroyed. I compliment the minister and the government upon that wise action. It would be well for the government to continue that good work and to create a similar reserve in the Teslin lake area in Yukon, abounding as it does in game animals, game fish, birds, wonderful scenery and all that goes to make the great outdoors attractive. Care should be taken to protect the timber in both those areas, timber which preserves the moisture in the earth, prevents the drying up of streams and forms a sanctuary for animal and bird life.
In this debate some hon. members have referred to the matter of the old age pension, and the subject is referred to in one of the amendments now under discussion. I have received many communications from old age

pensioners and from their associations complaining as to the terms and the method of administration of the act. At the outset the dominion government and the provincial governments bore the cost of old age pensions equally. Then the federal government assumed payment of seventy-five per cent of the pension, leaving twenty-five per cent to be provided by the provinces, which were also to administer the act. In my opinion, the federal government should pay the whole cost, 100 per cent of the old age pension, and also administer the act, and the pension should be at least one dollar a day. Those who receive pensions should begin to receive it at the age of sixty. At present the full pension is only $20 a month. Who could live on that? And the amount cannot be had until the applicant reaches the age of seventy, reaches the end of the allotted span of life, three score years and ten. In other words, he ought to be dead before he gets the pension.
Further, the period of residence in any part of Canada should count for pension. At present, if an applicant for old age pension has resided for fifteen years in Yukon and then five years in a province of Canada and is qualified for pension, a pension of only $5 a month is granted. That applicant has resided for twenty years in two different parts of Canada, and for more than twenty years perhaps in many other parts of Canada. In Yukon it has not been in the interests of those who might receive the old age pension to invoke the terms of the act. Unfortunate people needing pensions are cared for there at an expense greatly in excess of the old age pension of $20 a month, which is the maximum pension payable. That is all to the good for people remaining in Yukon, but it is most unfair to old people who have lived most of their lives in that part of Canada called Yukon and then moved to a province of Canada in their old age. Their years of residence in Yukon, Canada, are not taken into account, and the time of residence in Canada begins to run only with the date of residence in a province of Canada.
Another unfairness in the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act is that the period of residence in Canada after application made for pension does not* count for pension. For instance, a person having resided for only five years in a part of Canada where the act is operative and being otherwise entitled to pension is given a pension of only $5 a month. Then, if the person continues to live, no matter for how long, in that part of Canada in which the act is operative, the pension is not increased*, whereas if the applicant had

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
waited until twenty years had elapsed before making application for pension he would get $20 a month.

speechtext: He would be dead then.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He would have
reached the age of three score years and ten.
In all fairness I think the pension should be increased by SI a month for each year until the maximum is reached, and the maximum should not be less than $30 a month.
We read of all sorts of plans and schemes to make this old world a utopia after the war, a land of freedom from fear and freedom from want. Freedom from fear and freedom from want could be given immediately to thousands of unfortunate old people in this Dominion of Canada if this government is in earnest in wishing to bring about freedom from fear and freedom from want. A simple amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act introduced into this house at this session and put through, as I am sure it would be unanimously, would ensure to these old people freedom from fear and freedom from want. I would draw up a bill and introduce it into the house myself if that were possible, but under the rules of the house it would have to be introduced by a minister of the crown as a government measure. A private member could not introduce it. But I say to the government and to every one of the ministers that if they are serious in wanting to bring about freedom from fear and freedom from want to thousands of old people in this country, amend the pension act at this session. It could be very easily done, and I know the whole house would support it.
As I have said before in this house on a number of occasions, both at this session and at the previous session, the wage situation in Yukon is most unsatisfactory, due again to regulations passed by this government and administered by these regulatory boards and commissions.
This government has put a ceiling on wages that Canadian employers may pay and that their employees may receive. Foreign employers operating in Yukon are allowed to disregard that Canadian law, and they pay their employees working in Yukon much higher *wages than Canadian workmen receive, working side by side with them. The government of Canada has prohibited Canadian workmen in Yukon from earning those higher wages that foreign workmen receive in Yukon. I have said and repeat that in fairness to Canadian workmen, either the foreign employers should be compelled to comply with
Canadian laws while in Canada, or Canadian employers and employees should be allowed to pay and to receive as high wages as those paid and received in Yukon by foreign employers and employees.
To revert to the building of the Alaska highway, Yukon and the Atlin mining district of British Columbia are faced with a serious transportation problem. The operation of the railway from Skagway on the coast of Alaska to White Horse, the head of navigation on Yukon river, has been taken over under lease by the United States army. The operation of a mountain railway in the north in winter is no simple matter, and to be successful it must be handled by men trained in railway operation. Evidently the army men on that job have not been men with experience in operating railways, with the result that there has been and is a serious congestion of freight at Skagway. Thousands of tons of freight for the interior are piled on the docks at Skagway. Boats lie idle in the harbour waiting to discharge cargo for which there is no space on the docks. The population of Yukon has been unable to get supplies, as have also the people of the important mining camp of Atlin in British Columbia. Atlin being in the constituency of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson), the hon. member will bear me out in that. He has been appealed to as I have. Protests have been of no avail. Civilians were promised four carloads of goods a day over the railwTay. In forty-nine days they received only four cars. Perishables imported in plenty of time to have been delivered by Christmas were left on the docks in Skagway to freeze and were delivered only late in January, ruined and unfit for use. Not only i3 the civilian population of Yukon suffering, but the Department of Transport for Canada has had the same experience. If some corrective action is not taken by those in authority in the United States and in Canada the present hopeless mess will by spring be infinitely worse.
The season of navigation on Yukon river is for only about four and a half months. The great bulk of that delayed freight will have to be handled by river boats, but with the tie-up on the railway-an unnecessary tie-up- the boats will be waiting at the docks for freight, and the summer will be gone.
When Brigadier-General J. A. O'Connor, officer commanding northwest service command of the United States army of occupation in southern Yukon, came to Ottawa last month to present to the Prime Minister one blade of the golden scissors used to cut the ribbon at the official opening of the Alaska highway, I had the pleasure of meeting him, which

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
opportunity I owe to the hospitality of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie).
I discussed with General O'Connor and his staff the transportation situation brought about by the operation of the railway by the United States army. He frankly agreed that conditions had been unsatisfactory and promised that action would be taken to bring about improvement.
Since then, a conference has been held between Canadians and Americans at Edmonton, and it is to be hoped some progress will result.
It is in fact an appalling situation that needs immediate remedy. I appeal to the government of Canada and, through it, to the government of the United States to take action without delay, action to bring order out of chaos, action in the common cause.
An international committee has now been set up to study economic conditions in Alaska, northern British Columbia and Yukon.
The Alaska highway will open up new country. I am informed that already properly equipped prospecting parties are planning to explore areas served by the highway.
I do not expect to see any marked increase in agriculture in. Yukon. Field and garden crops grow wonderfully well, but owing tc the remote situation, the long haul to city markets, it has not been practical to grow more than enough for local consumption.
Mining has been and, as I see it, will always be Yukon's lifeblood. The magnitude of known deposits of gold, silver, lead and zinc ensure long life to the production of those minerals.
Last fall the dominion government's geological survey party, headed by Dr. Hugh Bostock of Ottawa, uncovered several outcroppings of scheelite and tungsten ore. Development work by those who staked the prospect uncovered a twelve-foot vein running high in tungsten values. Further work on that and other veins should result in at least one producing mine.
Geologists pronounce the Mayo mining district of Yukon as highly mineralized and recommend it as a likely field to prospectors.
Just to show what effect the advent of the United States army and American people and the building of United States projects in Canada is having on some people, I might mention that recently I saw that some visionary-I hope I have used the correct description-in the legislature of British Columbia, regretting that Yukon had escaped annexation by British Columbia, proposed the creation

of an international state of America comprising all the area north of the 64th parallel of latitude in British Columbia, with Yukon and Alaska thrown in.
As a Canadian I hope such a sell-out will never be considered by Canada. Speaking for Yukon, I am confident its people want Yukon to remain Canadian.
Mrs. DO RISE W. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford) : The budget debate has been before the house now for many' days, and the range and variety of the discussion have been wide. I believe that the people of Canada, generally speaking, have accepted this war-time budget as a part of their responsibility, and I think that acceptance is an expression of their desire to see a speedy offensive taken. The whole world has been waiting for the great offensive of the allied powers, and the ordinary people of this country are willing to deny themselves greatly in the hope that that great offensive will come soon. The longer it is left, it is becoming more apparent, the more we shall be playing into the hands of the enemy, whose greatest desire from the beginning has been to isolate, to weaken and then to destroy the united nations one by one. Any leaving of the great offensive now will be just a continuation of appeasement and will most assuredly help Hitler rather than help us. If, as time goes on this spring, a concerted offensive of the united nations is not taken, there will, I believe, be widespread disappoint nent among the people of this country.
Listening to this debate, I have been able to agree with points of view expressed by hon. members on both sides. Since, however, I am in the fortunate position of being an independent member, without party ties upon me, I find that I am most concerned and intend, in this debate, to speak mostly about the budget in its relation to my own people.
To my constituents and, no doubt, to many Canadians all over the country, the astronomical figures given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) mean very little. The figures of Canada's income, her assets and her spending are so enormous as to be almost incomprehensible to the majority of people. From my part of the country the figures of income and of income tax returns will not be astronomical by any means. But without doubt there has been a slight rise in income among our farming people; very small, however, if it is compared with the rise in income in the industrial areas of the country. Especially when one considers the rise of income compared with rising costs of living, the excess of income is very small. I believe more of my people than ever before will be

The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen
paying income tax this year, but there will still be many hundreds of them who do not yet come within the income tax brackets.
In the northwest corner of Saskatchewan, in my part of the country, there is no city of any size. We have a number of fair-sized farms in the southern area, in quite long settled farming districts. Further north are the small farms, the rehabilitation areas and the homestead districts. All through that country there are business men, storekeepers and so on in the little towns and villages. Then we have the professional people, the teachers and doctors; and last, but of course not least, the government inspectors!
I am unfortunately unable to give exact numbers, for figures are not available, but without doubt hundreds of families have left my part of the country, families who, feeling that their contribution on the farms was not worth while owing to the fact that the farms were small and their resources also small, have moved either to the coast of British Columbia or to eastern Canada and there have taken part in industrial work.
Speaking generally, I should like to emphasize the difficulty in the computation of income tax on the farm. Farming people are subjected to sudden losses. They never know from one year to another what their returns will be. They have to contend with the weather, insect pests, sudden losses through disease of stock. All these things make it particularly difficult for a farmer to have what might be called an average income or to know from year to year what his income will be. In the submission made this year to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by the Canadian federation of agriculture there was a section upon income tax which I should like to quote. It said:
As the provisions of the income tax have been widened, so as to make many farmers subject to it, many difficulties have been disclosed in applying the income tax equitably to farm income. We must commend the action of the government in setting up a special committee for the study of specific problems involved and feel that the work our representatives have been able to accomplish with that committee will prove to be of very considerable benefit. Continuing attention of administrative officials will be required to these agricultural problems. One fundamental principle requires legislation-
This is what I wish to emphasize:
the need for averaging agricultural income over a period of years for income tax purposes, which principle is quite essential to any fair application of the income tax because of the variability of farm income. We are aware that the act was amended at the last session of parliament to provide for setting off a loss incurred in 1942 against 1943 income. We recommend that the act be amended to make
that provision applicable to losses in 1941 as applicable to 1942, and establishing the general principle of averaging farm income over a period of more than two years.
I strongly support and urge other hon. members to support the principle embodied in that presentation. I believe that many of our farm people, when they realize that this government is willing to wait over a period of maybe some years for the balance of the 1942 income tax from those in the higher income brackets, will feel that the government could wait for a year or two also for an average computation of their income.
I believe also that more attention could be given to the question of the amount of depreciation allowed the farmers, not just for one year or even two. I believe all western members will support me in saying that western farmers have had to put up with the depreciation of a decade without receiving any real recognition of it.
There is another aspect of depreciation which I want particularly to bring before the house, namely, the question of human depreciation. This year we are asked for tremendous increases in food production, which will require on the part of our farm people almost superhuman effort. On most farms there are some machines, human machines, which have received absolutely no consideration. The machine to which I refer is commonly called by the farmers " the missus." Lack of hired help has in thousands of instances resulted in the farm wife having to take over and step into the breach left by the hired man and the casual help being called either into the armed forces or into industry.
Let me try to give some idea of what it has meant in the way of extra work for farm women this winter. It has meant that they have had to rise an hour or two earlier in the morning, getting up by lamplight, dressing in thick coats, socks, overshoes and mitts to go out into the darkness to milk the cows, then hurry back to the house to get breakfast for the children who go to school, afterwards bundling up again in all their clothing to go out looking after the poultry and feeding the calves and hogs. In addition they have their routine work to do which is usually much heavier than that of their city sisters. Baking and churning have to be looked after. In many instances their husbands have to be away during the day, perhaps cutting wood or doing other things that have to be done on the farm. This means that the women have to do all the chores. They have to get out in the afternoon again as the wintry day draws in to look after young stock, maybe chase the
The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen

stock because it so often happens that when the woman is left alone, the stock will get out of the stockyard into feed stacks. There is water to be brought from the well, often pulled by hand, without a pump, milking and separating, feeding the calves, and bedding the animals for the night. During the spring work when the man has to be out on the land the woman has to do all these things. Besides that, she will often have to get out on the tractor or drive the horses, and maybe act as midwife to the old sow. All these things come in the day's work.
During the last ten years farm women have received very little consideration. There has been so little to go around when it comes to sending off an order to the mail order house, that it was the children who had the clothing so that they could go to school, the husband who had warm clothing, too, and a new ploughshare, or maybe a new harness. All these things come before the needs of the mother of the family.
I suggest that when the farmer comes to fill out his income tax form he should do one of two things. First of all, if the farm wife is doing the work formerly done by a hired man, her husband should put down in the income tax form a claim for wages, quite substantial wages, for his wife.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And pay her the wages.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or, alternately, he should put down a substantial claim for depreciation of the very best piece of farm machinery a farmer has, a good wife.
It is the same with the farmer's daughters, they also are going without many things which they should have. Many of these girls have given up the last year or two of high school to stay at home and help on the farm. We have heard about the "forgotten man", but I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the forgotten women of this country, the farm women, wives and daughters. Many of these girls would like to join the auxiliary forces, get in uniform, but they are forgoing these things and staying home on the farm and [DOT] getting absolutely nothing for it. Mention was made of this fact in the same brief from which I just quoted:
Due recognition is also required for the work of members of the farm family in producing farm income.
I am the only farm woman in this house. Were I to give to-night my whole forty minutes to the question of farm women, I still could not do them justice; I could not make clear the great debt which the people of the United Nations owe to the farm women

of Canada for carrying on. Listening this afternoon to the speech of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), I could not help noticing the difference between the assistance given to the large corporations of this country and that given to our farm people. Our farm people are most willing to pay their fair share-I wish to underline the word "fair". Taxation; yes, they are willing to accept taxation; they are not trying to dodge anything. They do want to know that they are contributing their share toward the winning of the war. But another matter that worries them is how they are to live not only through the war period but in the years to come after.
It is generally acknowledged, I think, that for at least a few years after the war is over we shall be needing supplies of food, breeding stock, seed and things of that kind which the farmers will be able to supply to the people of Europe. But that period will not last for so very long, and what then? What hopes or what knowledge of security have our farm people to go on, or what have they been given by way of definite assurance by this government? I would refer to one more section of the submission by the Canadian federation of agriculture, which I should like to impress upon hon. members. It is under the sub-heading, "Price Ceilings", and reads:
As pointed out to your government in our submission last year when the government decided to embark upon a price ceiling policy in Canada, it so happened that the base period which was selected was one in which agriculture was at a disadvantage, and the ceilings for some of our principal agricultural products were far too low. Some substantial price adjustments have been made, but agriculture has had to struggle with increased costs which have to a considerable extent offset the benefits of these adjustments. As we stated in our submission to the government last year, "'Canadian agriculture can contribute its full share to the national war effort only when prices of agricultural products bear a fair relation to the prices of industrial products the farmer lias to buy." We therefore reaffirm our position with respect to parity prices as expressed in last year's submission.
Our farming people are concerned with these things; they have to be, because they have known a struggle for existence during the last decade. I have no hesitation in saying that they fear the future. They fear the future if we should lose the war, yes; but still even if we win the war our farming people fear the future, unfortunately. The people of my own particular area are aware of the fact that they cannot look upon the future with any hope if agriculture continues on the same basis as in the past. The people of Saskatchewan are hoping that they, and particularly the boys who return, may have something

The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen
other than agriculture to which to turn. During these days we hear a great deal about the Alaska highway, of the new' vistas which it opens, the new enterprises which are being started, the prospective new cities which are to be built, all in northern Alberta and British Columbia. Unfortunately we do not hear anything about northern Saskatchewan. Only the other day I looked through the report issued by the government of Saskatchewan as to the natural resources of that province, and there I found very little mention of any new developments, though there was a ready acknowledgment of the very rich ore deposits of northern Saskatchewan. Some time ago, in fact in November, 1941, I came across a copy of the Canadian Mining Reporter published in the city of Toronto, containing a front page article with regard to big oil developments in our province. I should like to quote a portion of it:
The many farmers of the province of Saskatchewan who have suffered through the lean years of depression, drought and the other plagues of agricultural life, as well as the merchants, traders, and others for whom agriculture is the basic means of life are filled with new hope and high expectation to-day. The news first given in the columns of the Canadian ilintng Reporter in our last issue that the Bobjo mining interests have secured a reservation of between four and five thousand square miles and are now busily engaged in the search for oil in Saskatchewan has had electric effect, if one may judge by the follow-ups of our story appearing in Canadian daily papers. This story of Bobjo s far-seeing enterprise is not the most encouraging that might have been told. The fact that Imperial Oil Limited has been granted a reservation of one million acres by the Saskatchewan provincial government is of even greater significance, remembering the outstanding character of that company, its long and wide experience and its mastery of every scientific method in seeking oil.
In my opinion it was a most dastardly thing that the province of Saskatchewan should give a million acres of land to Imperial
Oil.	How much more in the interest of our people would it have been for the dominion government to supply the provincial government with funds so that the natural resources of that province might be retained for the benefit of its own people. While this article was published in November, 1941, even now in 1943 we hear little or nothing about the development of oil in northern Saskatchewan; yet had this been carried on as a national enterprise, we might now be producing oil there. How do we know when Imperial Oil will be ready to commence operations? In the meantime that vast resource, which should be used in the interests of the people of Saskatchewan, lies undeveloped.
The people of my province must find new uses for agricultural products, too. Chemurgy
must find new uses for farm products; industries must be opened up. Vast works programmes should be developed for Saskatchewan boys who will return when the war is over. We do not want any more reestablishment schemes up in that part of the country; we have tried them, and the people have no use for them. In addition to employing men as miners, men would be required as builders, construction workers, railway construction workers, and road builders. For some nine years now we have had the beginning of a railway through the Pierceland area to link up with that part of Saskatchewan and the city of Saskatoon with Edmonton, but that road runs to nowhere; it is unfinished. It is time developments of this kind were undertaken to link up the farming district of the north with the developments which will take place in Alberta and British Columbia. Think of what those developments could mean to the people of my part of Saskatchewan. Our farmers would be able to supply the miners and workers in that area with meat, eggs, butter, milk, fresh vegetables and so on-at parity prices, it must be remembered-and there would be markets for all the various products of the mixed farming area. The city of North Battleford itself, which does not happen to be within my own riding but which is the natural centre of that area, could very well have had this year a government-owned and operated abattoir and packing plant to take care of the vast numbers of cattle and hogs which are coming down from the north and many of which must now be diverted right through to Winnipeg, which means a loss to our farm population through shrinkage and in other ways.
After all, these people are making a great contribution. They will continue to make a great contribution, but they would like some security. The small town business men and storekeepers are also concerned, not only with the present but with the future. I have been receiving letters from numbers of them, pointing out the difference between the treatment accorded the small retailer in Britain and that meted out in this country, pointing out that the small retailer and the consumer in our widespread country areas are threatened today, and the need for their protection. I am in agreement with that, and I would urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to see that the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board ensure that stores in these small towns and villages throughout western Canada receive their share of goods according to population needs, and not merely as the operation of commercial competition allows. There is a great need for the protection of the small
The Budget-Mrs. Nieben

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And no Easter bonnet?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, and no Easter bonnet, either, because that type of person does not exist out there.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have
no hesitation in stating that I intend voting with the government at the end of the budget debate. This budget, it is true, will mean an enormous burden for the Canadian taxpayers to shoulder, but

The Budget-Mr. Poirier
it will be borne for the most part, as it should be, by the richer citizens and let it be said to the credit of the government and of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), that the working clas9, the agricultural class and the small taxpayer generally are in a position to pay the taxes which are being asked of them in order that we may win this war and that they ask nothing better than to contribute to this country's war effort providing their income is reasonable. Let us take the farmer group, for instance. The farmers in the province of Quebec generally are satisfied with the prices for farm products w'hich have been set by the wartime prices and trade board. Certain improvements might be possible, to be sure, as in the case of hog prices. Farmers claim they cannot raise hogs for sale at $17.50 per 100 pounds. A little good-will on the part of the board could easily remedy this situation. The price should be fixed at $22.50 to $23 per 100 pounds.
The price for butter at 35 cents on an average for the past twelve months is satisfactory, particularly if we add the summer bonus of 6 cents per pound and the winter bonus of 10 cents per pound of fat, which is paid by the federal government. I believe farmers in the province of Quebec find these prices quite satisfactory.
Another price which is reasonable is that of eggs, which has stood in my district at 25 to 45 cents per dozen since last August.
The same holds true of all other farm products. When I state that a price is reasonable, I mean a price which leaves a profit to the farmer and entails no undue hardship for the consumer. A fair balance must be struck and such is what is being achieved in most cases by the wartime prices and trade board.
Let us now examine what farmers and workingmen are paying for the principal foodstuffs they buy and compare with the prices which existed in 1917-18.
The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) stated in the house the other day that a price of $4 per 100 pounds is being paid for flour. This ini no way corresponds with prices recently published by the Federated Cooperative Society of Montreal. Bread flour is quoted per 100 pounds as follows: cooperative flour, first quality, $2.40; federated flour (choice bread patent), $2.15; nutrition flour (85 per cent whole wheat), $2.15.
Any farmer can buy directly from the Federated Cooperative. As you see, Mr. Speaker, some of those who criticize the government take advantage of your good faith and that of this house.
Let us remember that in 1917-18 flour was paid as high as $9 per 100 pounds and sugar up to $28 per 100 pounds. The retail price of sugar to-day, after three and a half years of war, is 8i cents a pound.
As for wheat and wheat products and feeds generally, I am of the opinion that, contrary to what the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains has claimed, that prices are also very satisfactory.
On September 17 last the Federated Cooperative was offering wheat No. 5 in bulk at $1.28 per 100 pounds to Quebec and eastern Canada farmers and we know that the Canadian government pays freight charges from west to east on bran, shorts, middlings as well as on barley and oats.
Ground wheat sells to farmers for $2.10 per 100 pounds, ground barley for $2 per 100 pounds; plain dairy feed for $2.15 per 100 pounds; early chick mash, $2.95 per 100 pounds; growing chick mash, $2.60 per 100 pounds and laying mash, $2.60 per 100 pounds.
In most cases, these prices are even lower than pre-war prices and I feel that they are reasonable when compared with those which the farmer is getting for his products.
I have a suggestion to offer to the Department of Finance. In my constituency of Bonaventure, as in many rural constituencies of the province of Quebec, a large number of farmers' sons and of fishermen work in the bush during the winter, which is the slack season. The majority of these young men do not earn $750 in a year and therefore are not subject to income tax. However, in all cases, the tax is deducted at the source. I know that the government has announced in the newspapers that the tax thus collected will be refunded upon presentation of a claim, but when the individuals concerned ask for claim forms they get no answer, or else they are told that the forms are not yet printed. The government should have claim forms sent to all rural post offices and advertise that fact in the newspapers and through the radio.
May I be allowed to make a few more observations with special reference to the county of Bonaventure which I represent in this house?
During the present war my constituency has supplied approximately 2,500 men through voluntary enlistment to the three branches of our armed forces. Moreover, district No. 5 has called at least 1,000 draftees for military service in Bonaventure county, and we have nearly 1,000 men in the reserve army. This latter group of men is commanded by a hero of the great war, Colonel Dupuis, and is being trained in a very scientific and modern
The Budget-Mr. Poirier

manner. They are becoming more proficient in handling rifles and machine guns. You will see. Mr. Speaker, that they will defend Gaspesia if it is ever attacked. Bonaventure county has thus sent to date nearly 4,500 men to the three services of the Canadian armed forces out of a population of 42,000. I believe that about 40 per cent of the callable men in my county, who are 19 to 45 years old, have answered the call to arms. We have made this war contribution wholeheartedly and with a generosity that is not to be found everywhere.
We have given more than our share and I would call the attention of the authorities to the fact that it would be dangerous to ask much more of us in the circumstances.
I would point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), who is in charge of the mobilization of recruits, that notwithstanding the facts which I have referred to and in spite of the instructions recently sent to the registrars of military district No. 5 by the deputy minister, Mr. MacNamara, they are still calling the farmers' and the fishermen's sons in Bonaventure county.
As I have said the sons of farmers and fishermen who are left are absolutely needed for farming and fishing, and, if a greater number of our boys are called for military service the national life of our section would be endangered. I beg of the minister to put a stop to the ill-advised zeal of the district No. 5 registrar who, living 500 miles away from Gaspesia, is not aware of the conditions which exist in our primary industries. We must absolutely keep the remaining farmers' and fishermen's sons if we are to harvest from our farms and our fisheries, and from our forests what our country expects of us. The registrar of district No. 5 should not ask so much of Bonaventure and Gaspe counties and a little .more of the other sections of his district.
Mr. Speaker, once again I say to the house: Bonaventure and Gaspe counties generally are not treated under the confederation pact as they should be. In this war, as in the great war, our boys were the first to enlist voluntarily in the Canadian forces; 300 young men from Gaspesia have either shed their blood at Hong Kong or are prisoners of war in that distant stronghold. Nevertheless, during the last fifty years, our excess population had to seek other skies to earn its living.
Notwithstanding a substantial natural increase, our population has been practically stationary for over fifty years, because our means of communication are inadequate, because our natural resources, our mines, our fisheries and our agriculture are not thoroughly

developed; we lack capital. I take this opportunity to invite Canadian or foreign investors alike to come and invest money in the Gaspe-sian area; they will find there people that are both hard-working and law-abiding.
As a first remedy for present conditions, I would ask the government to show more interest in our railway; one might hardly believe it, but our trains in Gaspesia are still rolling, in 1943, on 55-lb. rails. The road-bed needs ballast to withstand heavy war-time traffic, which could raise a much more urgent problem should the Gaspe region be subjected to enemy attack, and that is quite possible. I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud) who, represents the neighbouring constituency of Restigouche, to give sympathetic consideration to this problem. After all, Mr. Speaker, I am not asking for any favour; our Gaspesian railroad is one of the very few sections of the Canadian National Railways that show profits each year, in spite of its poor condition; therefore it would be a paying proposition for the government.
As a second remedy to our abnormal situation, I would ask the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) to have the Gaspesian subsoil seriously explored. We have oil fields as well as zinc and lead ores, and so forth. So far, researches have been entrusted to the Imperial Oil and the Standard Oil, who have the best possible reasons at the present time for leaving those Gaspesian oil-fields undeveloped ; of course, they have not struck oil nor will they do so as long as they see no benefit to be derived from it. I suggest that the Minister of Mines and Resources, in Ottawa, should have thorough surveys made and should take an interest in the development of the Bustejd mine and the Federal mine in Bonaventure county, and also in the development of oil fields of Gaspe county. This has often been asked for by my hon. friend, the member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy).
As a third remedy, I ask the Department of Fisheries to continue and increase the assistance granted these many years for the establishment of fishermen's cooperatives. Cooperatives wall be, essential to the Gaspesian fisheries after the war. If cooperatives survive, our fisheries will prosper. If cooperatives fail, our fisheries will gradually disappear. I suggest that the government double its $8,000 subsidy to the St. Anne social service toward setting up fishermen's cooperatives.
I also ask the Minister of Fisheries to provide for the production of herring oil and fishmeal. Huge quantities of herring oil are now required for war purposes. If only given the opportunity to market their product, Gaspe coast

The Budget-Mr. Poirier
fishermen can catch vast quantities of herring. The Nadeau Laboratories, of Montreal, which already have plants in the Gaspe peninsula for the extraction of cod liver oil, are prepared, with government assistance, to take up the extraction of herring oil. To this day, the Canadian government has not spent a single penny on war industries in my county. I feel we should have a small share of the huge sums that are being lavished on other districts.
Finally, as a fourth and last remedy, I suggest, with regard to farming, that the government cooperate more and more with the Quebec department of agriculture and colonization with a view to facilitating the establishment of farmers' sons in the Gaspesian areas of settlement. We hear about post-war immigration. I object and will steadfastly object to any immigration policy unless and until jobs have been provided for all Canadians and until all our returned men are established on the land or in industry.
' Our soldiers who are farmers' sons must be settled on farms after the war and this requires the full cooperation of the dominion and provincial governments. The federal government must assume a large share of the financing of this project. Why should it not do so instead of paying for the settlement of immigrants?
Befrn-e closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a few paragraphs of the remarkable speech delivered last February 25 in the Quebec provincial house by the Hon. Adelard Godbout, premier of my province. All who heard him on that occasion, Mr. Speaker, are agreed that he had never before reached loftier peaks of eloquence. I am proud, Mr. Speaker, of the premier of my province and it is my belief that, in these critical times, he faithfully represents the feelings of the average and enlightened section of the French-Canadian element. I believe furthermore that the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe was well inspired in leaving him the mantle of leadership and that he is in all respects worthy of the great Liberal leaders who have governed Canada and the province of Quebec for nearly half a century. Here then are Mr. Godbout's closing words:
When we have formed an educated, cultured and strong youth, we shall be secure against many crises, adds the Premier. A deep understanding of public and social needs is essential to this end. We must strive for unity in the province and in Canada. We must not work under the delusion that we have all rights and no duties. We are called to live with the other provinces. Had God been an out-and-out racist we should still be Gentiles. Let us maintain our rights with tolerance and moderation. For the French Canadian I claim equal rights and I promise that, on national questions, my province will march side by side with the rest. We wish to cooperate with Ottawa for our own salvation and for no other reason.
During the present conflict, the Premier stated he would not utter a single word that might incite racial hatred in Canada. During this most critical period of our history, it is the duty of every good Canadian to remain silent at times. While our workers labour in the factories, while our farmers draw the maximum production from their lands, while our soldiers fight for us on the battlefields, no one has the right, for petty political purposes, to utter any statements that might lead others to consider French Canadians as cowards. French Canadians contribute to the war effort to a greater extent than any other nation, in view of the special circumstances in which they find themselves and in spite of the attacks levelled at them.
I am proud of my own people's war effort. It is for my fellow-citizens that I am fighting in public life.
Canada, stated the Hon. Mr. Godbout, is an autonomous country, but with a mixed population. If we were to tell French Canadians that they have rights without duties, and that they must live isolated from the rest of the population, we would simply be leading them to their doom. As long as I shall be Premier, the province of Quebec will grant equal rights to everyone of its citizens, this is my pledge. My government wishes that the weakest may enjoy a larger share of protection and happiness. We -want to be given as an example to the other provinces and to the whole world. But never shall we exert an influence in this world if we are to remain poor and that is why we want to form a young generation better educated and more patriotic. Then French Canadians wrill have nothing to fear from anyone.
My country is not Quebec alone, but Canada concluded the Premier. And as a field of endeavour for my sons I want not only Canada but the whole of America and that is why I have taken in this war the position to which I adhere to-day and to which I shall adhere still more firmly until victory is achieved.
These words, Mr. Speaker, might as well have fallen from the lips of Laurier instead of from those of Mr. Godbout. If to-day French Canada's war effort is realized by those around us, it is due, and it will be due especially when this war is over, to the Hon. Mr. Godbout, to Cardinal Villeneuve, and to those representatives of my province who in this house, where I have the privilege to speak, follow such leaders.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I am pleased to congratulate the hon. lady member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) upon the gracious speech that she delivered the other day in French in this house. Our English-speaking fellow members cannot imagine how deeply we French Canadians feel those attentions from the majority just because we are the minority in this house. I wish to thank very much the hon. lady member and also to assure her that her name is now in all French-Canadian hearts.
Before I resume my seat, I am pleased to quote the opinion on our Prime Minister (Mr. REVISED EDITION
The Budget-Mr. Poirier

Mackenzie King) held by a newcomer to Canada, a man who came to Ottawa last January to represent the London Times, Mr. A. Inglis. In a long dispatch sent to his journal on February 10, he concluded in the following terms regarding our Prime Minister:
In spite of political acerbities arising from deep-rooted domestic and sectional problems, Canadian political thought is imbued with a spirited nationalism. The country is now well established as a distinct, self-contained constitutional entity, which found its fullest expression in Canada's independent declaration of war; and while British and French interests frequently run counter to one auother, geographical, historical, racial and economic factors have resulted in a synthesis that can only be described as Canadian.
It is his enunciation of this Canadianism that gives the Prime Minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, his dominating position in current Canadian politics. Long associated with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, he has taken to heart that statesman's dictum that the greatest task which a Canadian party leader can assume is to prevent a widening of the fissures between French and British Canada. The adherence to nationalism inherent in this belief enabled Mr. Mackenzie King to bring a united Canada into the war; and although domestic issues, particularly the plebiscite on conscription for overseas service, have disturbed that unity, they have not destroyed it. Canadians as a whole strongly endorse the policy of giving the fullest aid to the common cause and French Canadians, having agreed to conscription for home defence, are ready enough to defend their homeland, although they have their own ideas about the merits of conscription for overseas service. . . .
More might have been done by the government in power to convince the French Canadians of the need for conscription, but less would have been achieved in maintaining national unity had some one other than Mr. Mackenzie King' been Prime Minister when the conscription issue arose. Canadian politics rage round the Prime Minister with a vehemence which his public record scarcely deserves; for among his colleagues and opponents few are endowed with a political flair equal to his, and none possesses his qualities as a parliamentarian. The fact that he rather than his government is chosen as the target for political criticism only gives emphasis to the commanding position which he holds. . . .
His political shrewdness, his patient, prudent, and persistent efforts to harmonize racial differences, and his long service to his country in office, have certainly ripened his political attributes into a matured if unspectacular statesmanship, which has contributed notably to the allied cause, both in the home field and in the international arena. . . .
In the war against Hitlerism Mr. Churchill and Mr. Koosevelt have fired the imagination of the world by their genius as war leaders. Mr. Mackenzie_ King's leadership assumes a different form in response to a different problem. His leadership reflects an infinite capacity for taking pains to ensure that Canada will contribute in the fullest measure to the enemy's defeat and will play her distinctive part in designing a new world order.

Mr. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski): Mr. Speaker, the budget that is now before us is undoubtedly the most colossal and extravagant that has ever been brought down in the Canadian parliament. Obviously, a fit of imperialistic frenzy has seized the minds of the leaders of this administration. Such a state of mind, which is in keeping with our thoughtless and boundless participation in the present war, is verging upon hysterics. The country is being blindly but surely led to a most disastrous ruin. Our participation in the war, which we were told would be on a moderate scale, has become total and gives absolutely no consideration to the material and human resources of our nation.
Canada, with a population of 11,500,000, cannot afford to bear much longer the crushing burden laid on its shoulders by an antinational policy and the orgy of expenditure which we have witnessed especially since the election of March 26, 1940. To bankrupt the country is the order of the day for the out and out exponents of imperialism and the vultures of high finance. On the other hand, the greedy war profiteers loudly demand conscription in order to increase their scandalous profits and to further their shameful speculations. Such is their idea of patriotism and their way of serving Canada. They are little concerned with the blood being shed on the battlefields, provided they can under the guise of patriotism and devotion to the country, succeed in building up huge fortunes and gorge themselves while thousands of young Canadians are being killed in action for the defence of our so-called democracy. A great Canadian statesman said one day: "Patriotism is the last refuge of scoundrels". If I might paraphrase that statement, I should say that nowadays patriotism is the last refuge of shameless war profiteers.
In preparing his budget, the honourable the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) could have shown more concern for the plight of large families and lightened their tax burden. His duty was to afford them tax relief rather than crush them with new taxes. Large families are the greatest asset of- any nation and the surest factor of race survival. If certain European countries had understood that truth and especially if they had put it into practice, they would not at this time find themselves in the terrible situation where a low birth-rate has placed them. The figures of the 1941 census clearly show that large families are to be found especially in the province of Quebec. That province is therefore more affected than all the others by the budget now under discussion.

The Budget-Mr. d'Anjou
I urge our Minister of Finance to ponder the disastrous consequences that will follow the imposition of vexatious taxes on large families in this country and especially in the province of Quebec. I trust that after a close study, he will revise his budget so as to grant them a fairer treatment, more appropriate to their income and their capability to pay taxes.
The agricultural class to which we all owe so much from every point of view, should not be subjected to income tax. Its war eSort is already important and costly enough to justify exemption. With the greatest imperturbability, it is being drained of its manpower, when farmers' sons are sent to military training centres, although they have been solemnly promised exemption from military service. This unspeakable behaviour, creates for our good farmers such conditions that a number of them, feeling discouraged, leave the farms to which they are so dearly attached and on which they have worked so hard. There is no eight-hour day for the farmer. Often he labours through fifteen or even twenty hours. Rising with the sun, very often he retires long after it has completed its course. Among all our population, no other class is composed of such indefatigable and steady workers. The farmer therefore deserves, from every point of view, the greatest support and encouragement of the government and of all the hon. members of this house.
Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to call the attention of the government and the members or parliament to a question of such importance that our failure to consider it without delay and in such a manner as to settle it with all fairness, might have the most disastrous moral and physical consequences on the future of our country. I refer to the employment of young girls and married and widowed women in industrial plants and especially in war factories. The highest dignitaries of the church, the archbishops and bishops of the whole country, as well as the medical associations, have warned us of the dangerous conditions in which our Canadian women find themselves as a consequence of their employment in war plants. The importance and extent of this evil have roused our patriotic organizations, our agricultural societies, our young people's associations as well as a number of municipal and county corporations. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) have been swamped with messages of protest on the part of these various associations and public bodies. In view of this general outcry, it is the moral and imperious duty of the government to institute a thorough inquiry in 72537-95J
this matter by persons whose qualifications are generally recognized and who will be in a position to recommend the best possible means of remedying this deplorable situation. Following such an inquiry the government would be acting in the best national interests by implementing the recommendations submitted to them.
In support of what I have said against the employment of women in war plants, I wish to quote a few excerpts from a most timely article which an outstanding Jesuit, Father Alexandre Dugre has written on that grave problem under the caption "A plea on behalf of Canadian women". I quote:
There is a marriage that will never take place; that of the young lady who has ruined her health working in a munition plant in order to earn some money for the purchase of clothes with a view to getting married. After six months of slow poisoning, she is debilitated, sallow-complexioned, exhausted, underweight, incurable, and she has not one cent for medical treatment. She has been an habitual visitor at hospital dispensaries; her suitor no longer sees her, offended by her new manners that are too vulgar and the parish priest has heeded her despairing cry which she would direct at all Canadian women for the charitable purpose of warning them.
And further on;
Gullible girls will no longer believe the deceitful propaganda of newspapers who show smiling, well-dressed, elegant young ladies among shells, at work benches or tending greasy machines. Why, they dirty their faces like men, and it is uglier because least expected; that is not a proper environment for them. The gullible ones will learn that salaries are higher in Ontario than here for the same working hours and the same kind of labour; that the most dangerous work is done in Quebec; that the selective service which claims to offer a variety of jobs scarcely offers to our Freneh-Canadian women anything but munition work, reserving for others the good office work at a high salary; that if the services of women are always needed, it is because the number of women workers who leave their jobs brings up quite a problem; a plant must replace on an average 1,200 women every month, and there is a reason for that; that what has ruined the 'health of another woman in six weeks or six months will also ruin yours if you enter the grinding mill-
And further on:
To work at night, in .violation of the law, during eleven hours and a half, in draughty rooms, to go from overheated places to damp and cold halls, to handle powder which gives off noxious fumes and explodes unexpectedly, to carry heavy burdens which cause a fall of the stomach, to breath dust, the odour of rubber, of tobacco, of powder, of mercury, of banana oil paint, of chemicals that are a frequent cause of burns, that is all in the day's work. As regards explosions, fatal or otherwise, all are bound, under oath, to say absolutely nothing about them. As regards normal or shameful diseases, they are accounted for by the fact that certain prostitutes, shown to be positive,
