and on the verge of being jailed, leave their slums and enter the shops where they continue to ply their trade, contaminating men as well as the conversations and the atmosphere.
And, further on:
Woman is neither the slave nor the queen of machinery; she is the queen of the home, the educator, the present or future governess of what is best and noblest in this world, of that for which we fight: the human brood.
And, to conclude:
If women must work, let it never be more than forty-eight hours a week, never at night when feasible, and let us organize the control and if need be, the isolation of germ carriers. Let us first employ the men, never the mothers, and ensure the physical and moral health of everyone. We could not be more accommodating.
In this war where we count so little, we put up with inconveniences, rationing and sacrifices. We supply the money, we give our sons, our blood. But we shall not sacrifice our women: it would mean setting ourselves back twenty centuries. That Hitler may be broken, some better means must be found than breaking up our homes by adding to the long roll of martyrs in the shops.
The eloquent argument of Reverend Father Dugre, on behalf of the Canadian woman, would surely deserve to be recorded in full.
Once more, I hope the government will realize the importance of this matter and act accordingly. Time presses and we must act without delay or hesitation.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the youth of my constituency, my province and the whole country, I urge in all possible earnestness, that the government grant an amnesty to all those who, for one reason or another, have failed to report for military training. Most of them meant no harm, but were rather ignorant of the law and the consequences of their neglect. I see no reason why the present government should be less generous, less magnanimous than the Union government of 1918.
At that time, I had the honour of representing Rimouski constituency in this house. Then, as now, the chase for defaulters was on as it is at present in my constituency. The Rimouski gaol was filled to capacity with so-called defaulters, who, for the greater part, were farmers' sons. On a visit I made to them, I promised to* have them freed. At the very beginning of the 1918 session, I insistently urged the government to free those unhappy victims of the heinous conscription act of 1917. I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to be able to state that I won my case. Indeed, one week later, the iron gates of the gaol at Rimouski were thrown wide open and all these young martyrs, these innocent victims of an infamous law, recovered their liberty and could breathe the air of freedom.

I hope, therefore, that the government will be generous and will grant an amnesty to all the young defaulters in my constituency and in the whole country.
During this debate, Mr. Speaker, many hon. members opposite, not immediately to your left, but rather in front of me, when our participation in the war was under discussion, never missed an opportunity of making comparisons and of saying that the province of Quebec was not doing its duty in this war. Mr. Speaker, I maintain that the contrary is true. In Rimouski county there is a military training centre where 1,300 young men are being trained at present. Most of them are farmers' sons who would be more useful on their father's farm putting in the crops, but they have answered the call willingly and they are undergoing military training like the others. The province of Quebec has no lesson to take from anybody. Its sons, particularly those who spring from the race of which I am proud, are neither cowards nor poltroons. During the last -war, two of my electors won the Victoria Cross on the field of action, the highest decoration which can be deserved by a soldier fighting for England: Jean Brillant and Joseph Keable, two gallant fighters, two heroes from Rimouski county. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that the people of my constituency are neither cowards nor poltroons. The electors of the constituency of Rimouski are anxious to do their duty, but of their own free will, according to the promise made to them during the 1940 electoral campaign. They do not want compulsion; they do not want conscription. They want to act as free citizens and defend their country when the time comes, but not under compulsion nor especially by methods well known to everyone.
I deem it my duty, Mr. Speaker, to register a protest and to defend the province of Quebec against the attacks which are continually made against her in this house by those who contend that she does not do her duty. French Canadians from Rimouski, as well as from anywhere else in the province of Quebec, have not only freely provided soldiers for the defence of both Canada and Great Britain, but they have consistently taken an interest in war work, namely, in the Red Cross; in short, in every form of assistance they have been asked to give to those who are now fighting our battle. Therefore, I hope that certain hon. members-whether they come from the great province of Ontario or from other parts of Canada-who cannot say a word without criticizing the province of Quebec will pay

heed to my words. As for me, I shall never tolerate anyone in this house to hurl abuse at and insult the province of Quebec and claim that it is not doing her share in the present war.

This is a very important debate, Mr. Speaker, on the question that has been raised by my hon. friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation who is also the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I remember the days in 1933 when I asked his group a large number of questions, most of which have not been answered. I do not question his sincerity. I believe he is just as sincere as was his predecessor as leader of that group, the late lamented Mr. Woods-worth, who is remembered by all as a faithful, devoted member of this house. I could say the same of the hon. gentleman who moved the subamendment, and of each of my colleagues in this house.
This subamendment consists of four paragraphs. The first is rather preliminary, but here is the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group as enunciated in this subamendment:
. . . this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for the nationalization of the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war.
That is the first plank in their programme. Here is the second one:
and further this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their widows and dependents.
With this I would agree to a certain extent. We are all willing to do what we can for those who suffer the calamity of being blind. We have every sympathy for the veterans who fought for this country in any war, whether on this or another continent; I make no exception in that regard. But in my opinion the law should be more elastic. It is within my knowledge that some people do not benefit from the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act just because those in charge of that legislation think of the letter rather than of the spirit of the law. There are some people who are not totally blind, but who are blind in one eye and can hardly see with the other. If they can distinguish between light and darkness with one eye, they are not considered blind by the bureaucrats of the old age pension board. This is, of course, absurd. Such people should enjoy the benefits of that legislation.
The war veterans should be well looked after, but they should be looked after according to their experience and disposition to work.
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

The dominion service has suffered to a large extent because a preference has been given indiscriminately to all veterans. So long as a man was a veteran, he was supposed to be qualified for nearly all jobs. This is absurd. I do not say that the state has no responsibility for those who return from war. They deserve the consideration and support of the state to a very large extent, but I do not see what service we are rendering a veteran, or what service we are rendering the state, by giving a man a job for which he is not qualified.
The third paragraph of the subamendment reads:
: ' l ,a"d further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control 01 the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and fananee.
I have something else to say with regard to the second wish expressed in that resolution. While it mentions the blind and the veterans, there is no mention at all of those who are at present unemployed and who receive no contribution from t-he unemployment insurance commission. This is absurd. We are told that everyone must help to accomplish a total war effort. I know many people who are willing to give every effort, but they have no opportunity to do so. It is hard for them to get work, and there are some of them who have no work to do. They receive no contribution from the state. They do not need any contribution, and they are not asking for it. They are in good health, and they are willing to work, provided they are given an opportunity to do so.
If we examine the subamendment carefully we must put together the first and third paragraphs, because evidently there is some connection between the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war, and the extent to which the government has vested control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance. I remember the day when I suggested that the party should have a programme. I remember the day, too, when it was done, although I had no responsibility for the way in which it was done. At that time there was a suggestion for a Bank of Canada. Why? Because in other countries they had state banks. They have one in England-the old lady of Threadneedle street. In France they have *the Banque de France, controlled by the famous and notorious two hundred families. And in the United States-well, everyone knows about the banking system over there. There are national banks in many other coun-

tries, and we were told to ape what was done in those countries by making their system our own. The funny part about it is that Mr. Bennett stole the programme from the Liberal party and was responsible for the establishing of the Bank of Canada.
He got a governor, who was to have the humble salary of S30,000 a year, a man who was even greater because he recommended that the humble labourer should tighten his belt. This man, getting a salary of $30,000 a year, was to tell the humble labourer to tighten his belt. We laughed at him, and he never said it again. That man was R. B. Bennett's choice.
But that is not the reason why I am against the Bank of Canada. I was against it before the programme was stolen by Bennett. A good citizen wrote me from the place where James A. Robb was bom, and asked me why I said the other day that from 1924 until 1930 I supported my party because it supported my electors. The reason is obvious. Hon. members will remember that there was an election at the time, and they will also remember the platform of the Liberal party: "Vote for the Liberal party; it is reducing national debt and taxation." Therefore, in supporting such a party my constituents were paying less taxes, and the burden of the national debt was getting lower and lower.
I gave my support with joy, until the turn came, with the accession of Mr. Bennett to power. Then the Bank of Canada was established, and the Liberal party complained of the fact that Mr. Bennett had stolen one of the most valuable planks in its programme. The first thing done by the party, after Bennett left office, was to build a monument for the Bank of Canada, a very expensive building. Before that the Bank of Canada was in the Victoria building at the comer of O'Connor and Wellington streets. Afterwards it was moved to the sumptuous building it now occupies.
After that I was sorry to see the reserve that was kept in the east block, the building in which are the offices of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and in which the council room is located, transferred from the vaults of that building to those in the new Bank of Canada building. I can see gold only at a distance. It was put in well screwed-down boxes, but I saw that each truck was accompanied by a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This backing of Canadian dollars was transferred to the Bank of Canada from a place where it was under the direct guard of the Minister of Finance. And, sir,

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
I always thought when a guarantee to pay was given, such guarantee of payment was in the hands of the same person. But now, incredibly, it is the Bank of Canada which issues bank notes, and the guarantee is not at all in the hands of that bank. It is in the hands of an altogether different organization, namely, the foreign exchange control board. The guarantee is given by the Bank of Canada, but the reserve is in the hands of the foreign exchange control board. I speak from memory; perhaps something has been changed, because things are changed without knowledge of the members. However, I have been told that is the way in which it was done.
I read with care the speech on March 9 of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in which he said it was the belief of his party that the whole financial system should be a national system. I believe the same thing. But I remember, too, that on the coast, at Mont St. Michel in France there is a medieval monastery famous for its gothic architecture. Many visitors go there, but when they cross at low tide, the road is quite narrow, and they must not leave it or they will fall in the mud and be buried. That is how I understand things are at the present time. When we are in the wrong, should we proceed further, or should we come back to the right way and then continue?
My policy in matters of finance is that of Jim Robb. He never had a university education. He was a mill owner, a man who grew up under the shadow of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was a tr-ue friend of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He had an unusual gift, that of common sense in business. I recommend to all members the reading of one of the most famous reports made by a parliamentary committee of this house. I think this committee sat in 1928, and Jim Robb was a member. It made a thorough study of the monetary and banking system. This report should be the corner-stone of all discussions and debates on banking. Why? Because the arguments advanced there are good and1 sound, because what was said before that committee was not said by schemers, by cranks, by doctors of every description, but by men of experience who had assumed the responsibility of being faithful guardians of the exchequer of this country.
I am delighted that the Minister of Finance has come into the chamber. He knows the personal regard I have for him because we have been friends since he has been a member of this house. Our relations have always been the most pleasant, and if at times I say
things that may be hard to digest, I do not say them to hurt him. The subamendment is illogical. It states:
. . . and further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance.
They also want a full utilization of the Bank of Canada. So long as the Bank of Canada is in the hands of those who control it at the present time, it will serve no useful purpose. My humble view is that we should change the heads of the Bank of Canada, rather suppress it and come back to the time when the Minister of Finance was responsible to the house for the financial policy of the government. That is the true British form of government. That was the policy of Fielding, Sir Thomas White and all the other great ministers of finance. I am sure that if the present Minister of Finance were given an opportunity to continue the traditions of Fielding and Sir Thomas AVhite, he would do quite well.
In these days of irresponsibility everyone tries to pass the buck to someone else. The office of the comptroller of the treasury was created in. a moment of bad humour. Mr. Bennett found that he could not stand his own self and he said, "We will do that." He was for centralization, and it was also decided to establish the Bank of Canada. This was also the Liberal policy for a time, but for me the real Liberal policy is the policy of ministerial responsibility. How can a minister say that he is responsible to the House of Commons when I am denied information about the trips of the doorman of the Bank of Canada around the world with R. B. Bennett? The government objected to giving that; the Prime Minister rose to protest against my receiving that information.
How can we do anything about it? What do we know about the number of employees of the Bank of Canada? There is no bridge between parliament and the Bank of Canada. There is no bridge between parliament and the foreign exchange control board. They are mysterious organizations. They may be good or they may be bad, but we do not have the satisfaction of being informed on what is going on behind closed doors. I protest against that as strongly as possible.
My policy is not to give life to new organizations; it is to cut them short. If Graham Towers has nothing else to do, put him on relief and1 give him a taste of that. We should get rid of all these people of the Bank of Canada. Get rid also of the foreign exchange control board, and place the responsibility of carrying out these regulations upon the
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

shoulders of the Minister of Finance. He may choose whom he likes as his staff, but he will have to inform us about what is going on, and what help he has, and give us their names, functions, salaries, travelling expenses paid and so on.
I do not question the honesty of these people, but the fact is that the only man who has been fired from the Department of Finance was a man who stole some bonds years ago and was put in gaol. That is the only occurrence I know of where anyone has been put out of the service. They are all there, and the number grows larger and larger. Where and when will it come to an end?
Who is the member of parliament who can speak with knowledge of the policies of the Bank of Canada except from what we know by hearsay from the minister himself? Where is the member of the House of Commons who has any intimate knowledge of the working of the Bank of Canada Act and all the other regulations in connection with the bank, which we do not receive half the time? All we have is a meagre report from the Bank of Canada. But what do we know of the regulations of the foreign exchange control board? They were published in two volumes in a shapeless form -fortunately an index was supplied later- but who has ever read them and understood them?
There is another reason why I am against the proposal of my hon. friends. It is because their main policy is that which was advocated by Mr. Woodsworth in years gone by. That is the policy they enunciate now and have been doing in years gone by. They are against profit. I quote the words of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, as reported at page 1109 of Hansard of March 9. He said:
However, the unfortunate factor is that in normal times the main stimulus to economic activity is not defence of the nation or the good of the community, but the making of profit. To my mind that motive is wrong.
When a man works hard for a few dollars a day, lives within his means and succeeds in saving perhaps a dollar or two each day, and then puts it in a bank or buys insurance with it, that is a profit, and it is a legitimate profit. What is wrong, Mr. Speaker, is for my hon. friends to think of profit as always being an extravagant profit. I know there are extravagant profits; I know there are schemers of every description; I know that very well. But I would not say that is true of the majority of the Canadian people. I believe that the majority of the Canadian people from coast to coast are honest people who can compare
[Mr Pouliot.]
favourably with those of any other nation in the world, and they live on profit.
Moreover, where does taxation come from if not from profit? And if there is no profit where will you get your taxation? That is a question I put in 1933 to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I put it again in 1934, and it has not yet been answered. It cannot be answered very easily. And how will they run their scheme if nobody makes any profit and if no taxes are paid? I wonder if there is any member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, however brilliant he may be, who can answer that question.
And then, with no profit, and therefore no taxation, they are for the Marsh report which will cost two billion dollars a year. Where will they get the money to put it into effect? It is incredible; it is illogical, and that is one reason why I shall be bound to vote against the subamendment.
There is something else. Money is not only a medium. It may be a medium at times. Money is an accessory to a principal transaction which is barter. That is how money or currency, or stones in the stone age, has always been considered since the beginning of the world. A man would bargain a camel for two sheep, and he would pay the difference in stones.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW RATE OF POSTAGE ON POSTCARDS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW RATE OF POSTAGE ON POSTCARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intended to inform the house this afternoon that when the budget resolutions were before us I would move an amendment affecting the rate of postage on postcards, making it three cents instead of two cents.. I think I stated in the budget speech that the rate on postcards would not be affected, but after consultation with the Post Office Department I find that to leave the matter in that position would affect existing and proper differentials, and therefore I propose to make an amendment. The Post Office Department is obliged to make certain preparations, which unfortunately became public before I had an opportunity of informing the house, but I am taking the opportunity of doing so now.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
